  • Spoken punctuation. In a recording, somebody who says “new paragraph” or “comma” usually means the words, so they are written as words. If you recorded yourself dictating on purpose, check Obey spoken punctuation and commands (Alt+O): then “comma”, “period”, “new line”, “new paragraph” and “scratch that” work just as they do when you dictate. Commands that move the cursor are ignored, because there is no cursor in a recording.

Which model for which recording

The Speech model list shows every model on your computer, most accurate first: the two that come with QUILL, and any you downloaded in Dictation Settings, Speech Models (see “Better accuracy: optional speech models” earlier in this chapter). Here is how to choose:

  • Voice notes and dictated letters. One clear voice, close to the microphone. Moonshine tiny is built in, is the fastest by far, and does this well. Whisper tiny is the one to try if Moonshine mishears an accent.
  • Interviews and meetings. Several voices, people interrupting, someone further from the microphone. A downloaded model is worth it here. Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 is our first choice: it is the most accurate model we offer and among the quickest of the big ones. Whisper small, medium or large-v3-turbo are good too, just slower.
  • Lectures and talks. One voice, a long time, and plenty of special words. Parakeet again, or a Whisper model. Before you start, add the speaker’s names and terms to My Words and Phrases, and you will spend less time correcting.
  • Noisy rooms. A café, a car, a hall with an echo. The bigger the model, the better it copes: Parakeet, Whisper medium or Whisper large-v3-turbo. The two tiny models struggle with noise. OpenAI is very good with noise too, if you use your own key (see below).
  • Spanish. Choose Spanish as the language first. The built-in Whisper tiny knows Spanish, and so do Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3, Nemotron and the multilingual Whisper models. The list shows only the models that know the language you chose.

A model that is too slow for live dictation is fine for a recording: nobody is waiting at the end of each sentence. The estimate tells you the wait before you start.

How long it takes

How long depends on the model and on your computer. These are our estimates for a one-hour recording, worked out from the speeds we measured for each model, on a modest computer (two processor cores, 4 GB of memory) and on a more capable one (four or more cores, 8 GB or more):

Model Modest computer Capable computer
Moonshine tiny (built in) 6 minutes 3 minutes
Whisper tiny (built in) 19 minutes 9 minutes
Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 30 minutes 13 minutes
Nemotron 37 minutes 16 minutes
Whisper small 1 hour 49 minutes 46 minutes
Whisper large-v3-turbo about 6 hours about 2 and a half hours

For a real example: a three-minute recording took 10 seconds with Moonshine tiny, 20 seconds with Whisper tiny and 25 seconds with Parakeet on the computer QUILL is developed on, plus a few seconds the first time while the model loads.

Transcribing uses two of your processor’s cores, the same as dictation, so your screen reader stays quick. The model is put away a few minutes after the last transcription finishes, which gives its memory back.

Where the text goes
  • A new document. The transcript opens in a new, untitled document when it is ready. Nothing is saved until you save it with Ctrl+S.
  • This document, at the cursor. The transcript goes where the cursor is in the document in front, at the moment it finishes, as paragraphs of its own. Ctrl+Z takes the whole thing back in one step. If that document has been closed or is read-only by then, the transcript opens in a new document instead, and you are told why.
Several recordings, checking on it, and stopping
  • Several at once. In Browse, hold Ctrl and choose more than one file. They are transcribed one after another with the same choices, and each one arrives in its own new document. If one is already running when you start another, you hear “Added to the queue”.
  • How far has it got? Press Shift+F5 again. At the top of the window, Transcribing now says which recording it is on, how far it has got, and how many are waiting. Press Escape to close the window and let it carry on.
  • Stopping. In that same window, press Stop Transcribing (Alt+S). The recording being transcribed stops, any waiting ones are forgotten, and nothing is written into a document.
  • If you missed what it said. Shift+F9 opens Activity, which keeps every transcription this session, finished or failed, with the reason when something went wrong.
Which files it can read

MP3, M4A, AAC, WAV, Ogg, Opus, FLAC and WMA, and also the sound in an MP4 file and AIFF. QUILL reads all of them itself, using parts of Windows that are already on your computer, so there is nothing extra to download and no other program to install. Files with copy protection, such as some bought audiobooks, cannot be read.

Privacy, and OpenAI with your own key

With the models on your computer, nothing leaves your computer. The recording is read, not copied, and nothing is kept afterwards except the text.

If you have your own OpenAI key saved in Use My Own AI Key, OpenAI’s speech models appear at the bottom of the list a moment after the window opens. OpenAI is very accurate, especially with several voices, accents and noise, but it sends your recording to OpenAI, so it is never chosen for you, and it is never offered in Safe Mode. When you choose it and press Enter, a question says exactly what will be sent. The answer is No unless you choose Yes, every time. If you agree:

  • the speech in the recording is sent over an encrypted connection to OpenAI, about a minute at a time, with your own key, and the words come back;
  • OpenAI bills your account by the minute of audio;
  • the names in My Words and Phrases are sent as words to expect;
  • nothing goes through QUILL’s servers, and QUILL keeps no copy;
  • OpenAI’s own policies apply to what it receives; you can read them at openai.com/policies.

Please only send recordings you have the right to share, and that the people speaking in them have agreed to. The live model, gpt-live-transcribe, is not in this list: it is made for a microphone, not a file.

Messages you might hear
  • “meeting.mp3 was not found.” The file was moved or renamed. Choose it again with Browse.
  • “meeting.mp3 could not be read as a recording.” It is not one of the formats above, or it is damaged or protected.
  • “meeting.mp3 was read to the end, but no speech was found in it.” The recording is silent, or very quiet. Nothing is written.
  • “… could not be loaded, so this used the built-in engine.” A downloaded model would not load, so Moonshine did the work instead. Removing and downloading the model again in Speech Models may help.
  • “Stopped transcribing meeting.mp3.” You pressed Stop Transcribing.
  • “Could not transcribe meeting.mp3”, followed by the reason, for anything else. You hear the error tone, and the reason stays in Activity.

Transcribe on your computer

QUILL can transcribe entirely on your computer, with no cloud account and without uploading your audio. No AI account or key is required, and you do not need to turn on Artificial Intelligence to use it.

  1. Choose Tools > Speech > Transcribe Audio or Video (Offline)….
  2. Pick an audio or video file.
  3. Choose a transcript format: plain text, Markdown, or HTML.
  4. Keep working while it runs in the background. QUILL tells you when it is done and how many words it produced, and opens the result as a draft document you can edit.

The first time you transcribe or dictate offline, QUILL may need to fetch its speech engine and a model. It offers to do that for you. The Speech section later in this chapter explains models and engines.

Supported formats and FFmpeg

Supported formats. You can pick MP3, M4A, AAC, FLAC, OGG, Opus, WMA, WAV, MP4, M4V, MOV, MKV, WebM, or AVI.

If ffmpeg is installed, QUILL converts the file for you before transcribing, so you never have to make a WAV yourself. QUILL does not ship ffmpeg, but it can fetch it:

  • Tools > Speech > Download FFmpeg… downloads the official build (about 110 MB, with a progress bar you can cancel) and sets it up.
  • Or install it yourself once (for example, winget install Gyan.FFmpeg) and QUILL finds it on your PATH.

ffmpeg is open source (GPL/LGPL) and comes straight from the official builder. QUILL never bundles or redistributes it. Without ffmpeg, the whisper.cpp engine needs a 16 kHz mono WAV, while the Faster Whisper engine can handle the other formats by itself.

Captions and speaker labels
  • Generate Captions (Offline)… on Tools > Speech transcribes a file with timestamps and saves the result as SRT or VTT caption files.
  • Speaker attribution. If you download the “Small English with speaker detection” model (in Manage Speech Models), QUILL marks who is speaking when. Each turn is labelled “Speaker 1”, “Speaker 2”, and so on in the transcript, in bold in Markdown and HTML. It tells the turns apart; it does not name the people.

Transcribe Audio File

If you have AI set up, AI > Transcribe Audio File… sends a recording to OpenAI Whisper in the cloud.

  1. Choose AI > Transcribe Audio File…. A file picker opens.
  2. Pick the audio file. Supported formats: MP3, MP4, M4A, WAV, WEBM, OGG, FLAC (maximum 25 MB).
  3. Choose your options:
    • Language: detect it automatically, or pick a language for better accuracy.
    • Speaker diarization (uses Deepgram): works out who is speaking when. Each turn is labelled Speaker 1, Speaker 2, and so on, with timestamps. This needs a Deepgram API key set up in AI Hub.
    • Translate to English: transcribes audio in any language and gives you an English translation in one step (Whisper translation mode).

When the transcript is ready, QUILL asks “What would you like me to make of this?” and offers a short list of Transcript Actions, chosen to suit the recording. Pick one and QUILL turns the transcript into a finished document, such as meeting minutes, action items, study notes or a clean draft, and opens it for you to review and edit. Or choose “Just keep the transcript” to go to the viewer, where you can copy it, insert it at the cursor, or open it as a new document. If AI is turned off, you go straight to the viewer.

AI > Translate Audio File to English… goes straight to the Whisper translation, skipping the language step.

Transcript Actions

A transcript is rarely what you actually need. You want the minutes, the action items, or a clean draft. Transcript Actions make that last step one choice away. You can reach them in two places:

  • Right after transcription, in the “What would you like me to make of this?” chooser described above.
  • Any time, on text you already have, with AI > Transcribe Audio > Transcript Actions…. Paste in a transcript or notes (or select part of your document) and pick an action.

The built-in actions are:

  • Meeting Minutes: attendees, decisions, action items with owners, follow-ups.
  • Action Items: every task and commitment as a numbered list you can act on.
  • Executive Summary: a short briefing for leadership.
  • Interview Notes: questions, answers, strengths, concerns and an assessment.
  • Study Notes: a lecture or talk turned into organized notes.
  • Q&A Extraction: every question and its answer in clean Q&A format.
  • Clean Up & Draft: spoken rambling turned into a clean, readable draft.
  • Follow-Up Email: a warm, ready-to-send recap with next steps.
  • Key Quotes: the most notable quotes, word for word, with who said them.
  • Decisions Log: just the decisions made, each with its reason and owner.

QUILL puts the most likely ones first for the recording in front of you. A meeting with several speakers starts with Minutes and Action Items; a single voice starts with Clean Up & Draft. Every action is always there, though. The finished document opens in a new window, so your original transcript is never overwritten. Transcript Actions use whichever AI provider you have set up in the AI Hub.

Automate transcription with watch folders

A watch folder lets you set a rule once: drop a file in this folder, and QUILL deals with it. You will find the commands on Tools > Watch Folder.

The Watch Folder menu

  • Watch Folder Monitoring (in Settings)… turns on or off the automatic opening of supported files dropped into a folder you have chosen.
  • Watch Folder Profiles… sets the folder path, whether subfolders count, what happens at startup, and how often the folder is checked.
  • Watch Folder Queue… shows what is happening right now and the settings in use.

Watch folders are good for “drop and open” work: copy supported files into one folder and let QUILL open them in the background. They respect Do Not Disturb and run quietly.

Transcribing arriving audio

Each watch profile runs one action on every file it picks up. As well as opening, moving, copying, converting, running a macro or a sandboxed transform, and OCR, a profile can transcribe arriving audio. Any audio or video file dropped into the folder is transcribed on your machine with the offline speech engine, and a transcript is written next to it. Nothing is uploaded.

Choose the Transcript format in the profile:

  • plain Text (.txt)
  • SubRip captions (.srt)
  • WebVTT captions (.vtt)
  • Markdown (.md)

The caption formats carry timestamps. If the engine returns no timed parts, they fall back to plain text, so you never get an empty caption file. This needs no consent. If no speech model is installed yet, the profile tells you to download one from Tools > Speech > Manage Speech Models.

There is also a separate Transcribe audio (OpenAI Whisper) action for cloud transcription, once you have turned on AI and set up a key.

Making minutes automatically

A transcribe profile can also chain an AI Action onto each recording:

  1. In Tools > Watch Folder > Watch Folder Profiles…, point a profile at a folder (for example, Meetings).
  2. Choose a transcribe action (offline or OpenAI Whisper).
  3. Under Then make, pick a Transcript Action, such as Meeting Minutes.

From then on, every recording that lands in that folder is transcribed, and the minutes document is written next to it, with a name like standup-meeting-minutes.md. If AI is off or no provider is set up, you still get the transcript. The action step is skipped with a note, never an error.

The Watch Folders page in Settings

  • Enable folder watching by default starts watching your enabled profiles each time QUILL starts. It is off to begin with. Watch Folder Monitoring (in Settings)… brings you to Settings so you can turn it on.
  • Default watch folder: if you just want one folder where anything you drop gets opened, you don’t need a profile. Put the folder here, and QUILL opens each new supported file that lands in it. Blank to begin with.
  • Start watching automatically is the switch that watches your default folder, from the moment QUILL opens and for as long as it runs. It works on its own, so you can watch the default folder without turning on Enable folder watching by default, which starts your profiles. Safe Mode turns both off. Off to begin with.
  • Include subfolders: turn this on and files in folders inside your default folder count too. Off to begin with.
  • Process existing files on start: normally QUILL only opens files that arrive after it starts watching. Turn this on to have it open what’s already waiting in the default folder as well. Off to begin with.

Your profiles each have their own folder and their own Include subfolders, existing files and startup choices; these four only decide for the default folder.

  • Poll interval (seconds) is how often a watched folder is checked, from 2 to 300 seconds. The default is 5.
  • Watch folder: play a sound on each check plays a short tick every time the folder is checked, so silence means the watcher has stopped rather than found nothing. Off to begin with.
  • Watch folder: let results interrupt speech announces a newly opened file straight away, cutting across whatever is being said. Off means the notice waits its turn.

Speech

Tools > Speech is where QUILL keeps its on-device speech tools: the transcription and dictation commands you have already met, and the speech models and engines that make them work. You do not have to understand any of this to dictate. Come here when you want a more accurate model, a lighter one for an older computer, or a different engine.

Manage Speech Models

Manage Speech Models… lists local speech models with their download size, accuracy and speed, and helps you pick one that will run well on your computer.

  • The dialog opens with a one-line summary of your machine: its RAM, and whether a GPU was found.
  • Each model shows roughly how much memory it needs. A model too big for your RAM is flagged.
  • The best fit for your computer is marked “Recommended for your computer.”
  • A larger model warns you when there is no GPU, because it will be slow on the CPU.

Choosing what to do. Pick a model, then choose an action: Download this model if it is not installed, or Remove this model from my computer if it is. Before a download starts, QUILL warns you if there is not enough free disk space.

Downloads run in the background and show progress. You can keep working. A progress window shows a percentage and has a Cancel button you can press at any time, and QUILL announces progress as it goes. Cancelling cleans up the partial file. Models come over a secure connection from the Hugging Face Hub and are stored on your computer. Downloading is turned off in Safe Mode.

Manage Speech Models is the Dictation (Offline) tab of the Speech Settings dialog. When more than one local engine is available, it asks which Speech Engine to use. A Set as Default button (or a right-click option) chooses which downloaded model QUILL uses without switching engines. QUILL remembers your choice and uses it for transcription, captions and dictation.

Choosing a speech engine

Choosing a speech engine. QUILL uses the whisper.cpp engine by default. You can add two more optional engines, each by installing what it depends on:

  • Faster Whisper (fasterwhisper dependency): a faster engine for many languages. It runs inside QUILL and uses your GPU automatically when you have one.
  • Vosk (vosk dependency): a very low-resource, CPU-only English engine that runs on a ~40 MB model with no GPU. It is ideal for older or smaller machines where the other engines are impractical. Its models download from alphacephei.com (verified HTTPS, integrity-checked) through Manage Speech Models.

Each engine has its own models, so download a model after switching. All of them run entirely on your computer. Faster Whisper does not label speakers; for speaker attribution, use the whisper.cpp speaker-detection model.

Getting the offline engine

Download Offline Speech Engine… The private, on-device speech engine (whisper.cpp) is not bundled in the installer. The first time you use offline dictation or transcription, QUILL offers to download it for you: about 8 MB, checksum-verified, with a progress bar you can cancel. It is turned off in Safe Mode. You can also fetch it any time from Tools > Speech > Download Offline Speech Engine…, or from the all-in-one Help > Download Optional Components list described below. If you are upgrading from a version that bundled the engine, your existing copy is kept and keeps working, with nothing to download.

The installer does not include it and has no option to add it. In a portable copy you can also place the executable under tools\speech\whispercpp yourself. You do not need to install anything else or change your PATH. Then download a model from Manage Speech Models.

Offline dictation also needs microphone-capture support (the optional sounddevice package). If it is missing, QUILL tells you, and you can still use Windows dictation.

Download Vosk… Vosk is a tiny, very light offline dictation and transcription engine for older or low-memory computers with no graphics card. It is not bundled. Tools > Speech > Download Vosk (or the Optional Components list) installs it when you ask, checksum-verified and turned off in Safe Mode, from QUILL’s own verified download, falling back to the public package index. whisper.cpp stays the default engine; Vosk is the lightweight fallback when you need it.

Hugging Face Token

Hugging Face Token… on Tools > Speech is optional. QUILL’s speech models are open source (MIT) and need no Hugging Face account to download. If you fetch a lot of models and run into Hugging Face’s rate limits, a free access token raises them.

The first time you open it, QUILL explains the steps: sign in or sign up at huggingface.co, open Settings > Access Tokens, and create a token with the Read role. It offers to open the token page in your browser, and then you paste the token in. The box hides what you type, and the token is stored in Windows Credential Manager, never in a settings file. Leave the box blank to remove a saved token.

Cloud transcription providers

The offline engines keep everything on your machine. If you also want a cloud provider, for example OpenAI Whisper for its accuracy, install the OpenAI Whisper Transcription Quillin (a bundled extension) and set up an OpenAI API key in AI Hub. It then shows up as a provider on the Dictation (Online) tab of Speech Settings. That tab is kept apart from the offline engines, so local engines (install once) and cloud ones (API key, paid per use) are never mixed in one list. If no cloud provider is installed, the tab tells you how to add one.

Cloud providers are opt-in and never silent:

  • Audio is uploaded only when you choose to transcribe a file with that provider. Never offline, and never in Safe Mode.
  • The watch folder’s offline transcription always uses the on-device engines, so a cloud provider can never upload your audio automatically.
  • An extension that adds a provider contains no code and asks for no network permission. QUILL does the upload itself, through its own checked network path, so the extension never sees your audio or your key.

Developers can read more in the Quillin guide, “Transcription providers”.

The Transcription page in Settings

  • Transcription provider preference is Local first (the default) or Cloud first, for when you have both kinds of provider.
  • Show cloud transcription providers lists cloud providers beside the ones on your computer. On to begin with.
  • Auto-open Status Page on model download opens the Status Page whenever a speech model starts downloading. Off to begin with.
  • Status page refresh announcements is how often the Status Page speaks its updates: Quiet (the default) says nothing on its own, Normal speaks about every thirty seconds, and Verbose about every ten.
  • QUILL Whisperer safe mode lock stops speech-model downloads and retries while leaving the status pages working.
  • Voice commands (push-to-talk) and Voice conversation mode turn on the voice commands described in Chapter 8.
  • Voice recognition engine chooses what listens for voice commands: Follow main engine, whisper.cpp (accurate) or Vosk (fast, light), which suits always-listening best.
  • Four settings pace conversation mode, all in milliseconds, and 0 switches each part off: Conversation: pause before a command ends (ms) (2000 to begin with; 0 uses the engine’s own pause), Conversation: cancel window before acting (ms) (900), Conversation: keep listening after a command (ms) (3000) and Conversation: ‘still working’ tick interval (ms) (2000).
  • Conversation: your name (optional) lets QUILL use your name in its prompts, as in “Listening, Sam.” Leave it blank for plain prompts.
  • Conversation: speak prompts aloud speaks the welcome and follow-up prompts with your Read Aloud voice. It is off to begin with, so QUILL does not talk over your screen reader; the sounds and the status bar still tell you what is happening.

Download Optional Components (Help menu)

To keep the installer small, QUILL fetches several large or optional pieces only when you want them. Help > Download Optional Components… is the one place to see, get, test and remove them all.

Everything here is optional. The base app, and the SAPI 5 voices built into Windows, work without any of it, so download only what you need. In portable mode, components install into your portable data folder, so your whole setup travels with you on the drive.

What is in the list

The list puts the most important first:

  • Pandoc: document conversion for Word, ODT, EPUB and RTF.
  • PDF and Office text extraction (MarkItDown, pdfplumber and pypdf): lets Import read the text out of Word, PowerPoint, Excel and PDF documents without Pandoc or LibreOffice. Scanned or image-only PDFs still need File > Import > OCR either way.
  • The braille translation pack: liblouis tables and BRF profiles for the Translation submenu and for BRF and embossing export.
  • Dictation (offline speech): a guided setup covering Whisper.cpp, Faster Whisper and Vosk, described below.
  • Kokoro and Piper neural voices, and eSpeak NG and DECtalk voices.
  • Audio: export, playback & chapters: FFmpeg for exporting compressed audio, the mpv playback engine, and MP3 audiobook chapter markers, all in one place. Each piece is fetched only when its feature is first used.
  • The MathCAT math-speech engine.
  • Git and the GitHub CLI: portable fallback copies for Tools > Git and GitHub > Local Git and the Codespaces and Copilot commands on Tools > GitHub. The section “Downloading git and the GitHub CLI”, where this guide covers Git and GitHub, has more.
  • The Node.js runtime, for Node Quillins and the Developer Console’s TypeScript interface. It comes last, as the extra people use least.
  • Any non-English spell-check dictionaries.

Each row shows whether it is Installed or Available to download, and its size. Selecting a row shows a plain description of what it gives you and what it costs.

Download, Test, Remove and Set as Default

  • Download fetches a component you do not have yet, checksum-verified, with its own progress.
  • Test proves an installed component works, so you can trust it before you rely on it. A voice speaks a short sample so you actually hear it. The offline speech engine transcribes a spoken phrase and tells you what it heard. Tools report their version. If a component just needs one more piece, Test takes you straight to it: the guided engine-and-model picker for offline speech, or Manage Voices for a voice engine with no voice yet. An unfinished setup is not treated as an error, and QUILL only offers to send a bug report when a test really fails.
  • Remove deletes QUILL’s downloaded copy of a component and turns its features back off. Removing a voice engine you were using, for example, switches Read Aloud back to the system voice. It only ever removes copies QUILL downloaded, never a system tool or a shared install.
  • Set as Default: for a voice engine (Kokoro, Piper and the other Read Aloud engines), the Set as Default button here makes that engine, and a voice you pick from it, your Read Aloud default without opening another speech dialog. The button is only available for a component that can be a Read Aloud default, and only once it is installed. The same Set as Default is also in Manage Speech Models and Manage Voices (with a right-click option on the list), for the offline dictation model and for voices. Downloading a model or voice engine makes it the default automatically; use these when you want to switch back to one you already have. Voice previews stop cleanly when you move to another before the first one finishes.

Setting up offline dictation

The Dictation (offline speech) row opens a guided setup instead of a plain download. It takes you one step at a time, and a banner at the top always says which step you are on and the one thing to do next:

  1. Pick and install an engine: Whisper.cpp (light and fast), Faster Whisper (most accurate), Parakeet 3 (the most reliable for dictation, described earlier in this chapter), or Vosk (tiny, best for old or low-memory machines).
  2. Download a model. The best fit for your computer is already selected.
  3. Choose Test dictation to make sure it works, then set it as your default.

QUILL remembers the engine you chose, so the setup reopens where you left off instead of going back to the built-in engine.

Pandoc on demand

Pandoc downloads itself when you need it. You do not have to visit this dialog first. The moment you Import or Export a Word, ODT, EPUB or RTF document (or run Convert File) without Pandoc, QUILL offers to download the official, pinned build right there: about 45 MB, verified, with a progress bar. The conversion is ready as soon as it finishes. Plain text and Markdown never need Pandoc, which is why it is not bundled.

On a Mac

On macOS, several of these come from Homebrew rather than a QUILL download.

  • The braille translation pack download contains a Windows lou_translate program, so on macOS QUILL points you to brew install liblouis instead. QUILL finds a Homebrew liblouis by itself, so no download is needed.
  • Pandoc and Tesseract work the same way. Install them with Homebrew (brew install pandoc, brew install tesseract) and QUILL finds them.
  • LibreOffice, used to import older Office formats and Apple Pages, is found automatically at its standard /Applications/LibreOffice.app location on macOS (it is never on PATH there). Install it from libreoffice.org or with brew install --cask libreoffice if you need those imports.

Performance and Memory

QUILL is built to run all of its AI and speech features on a modest computer with no graphics card and not much memory. It does that by being careful with memory, never by switching features off. Two settings under Settings > Performance and Memory control it:

  • Unload idle models after (minutes) frees the memory used by an AI, read-aloud or dictation model you have stopped using. The next time you need it, QUILL loads it again by itself. Set it to 0 to keep models loaded until you close QUILL.
  • Low-resource mode (one model at a time) keeps only one model loaded at a time and prefers the smallest model that fits. It never turns off AI or speech. It loads them one at a time, so you wait a moment for a reload in exchange for using much less memory. On a machine with very little memory it turns on automatically and tells you once, out loud, so it never takes you by surprise.

You do not have to touch either of these. QUILL picks sensible defaults for your machine, but they are there if you want to tune how much memory it uses.

What you learned, and where to go next

You can now dictate with Live Dictation (Ctrl+F11), pressing it to start and again to stop, or holding it while you talk once you turn that on, with Locked Dictation (Ctrl+F9) or with Dictate (Offline), and teach QUILL your own words in dictation.md. You know that your words go where you started speaking, how to see them while you talk with Nemotron or OpenAI, how to say “correct that”, how to talk to the AI out loud, and what OpenAI dictation sends and how to turn it on or off. You can spell, select, correct and move by voice, put in snippets and Copy Tray slots, switch between English and Spanish with Ctrl+Shift+F11, keep a live transcript with Ctrl+Alt+Shift+PageDown, and dictate into other programs through Quill Inkwell. You can transcribe a recording on your own computer or with AI > Transcribe Audio File…, turn it into minutes or notes with Transcript Actions, and set a watch folder to do all of that for you. You also know where speech models, optional components and the memory settings live.

To practise with QUILL beside you, open Help > Tutorials… (Ctrl+Alt+F1) and try “Write by talking”. The same track, “How much QUILL says”, also has five short dictation lessons: “Punctuation and symbols by voice”, “Fix a word by voice”, “Snippets and clips by voice”, “Switch to Spanish and back” and “Make a live transcript”. Each takes a few minutes, with QUILL telling you what to say. The Dictation commands page and the Voice Interaction guide are the best companions to this chapter.

Next, Chapter 10, AI, when you want it, shows what the assistant can do with your writing, including the AI behind Transcript Actions.

Chapter 10: AI, when you want it

This chapter is about the AI help built into QUILL, and the first thing to know is that you never have to use it. QUILL is a complete editor without it, and nothing you write is sent anywhere until you ask. If you would like a paragraph summarised, tidied or explained, QUILL’s own free AI is ready with no account and no key. If you already pay for ChatGPT, or have your own key, you can use those instead, and further on you will find the library where you can save your own prompts, skills and agents.

QUILL’s own free AI

You do not need an account, a key, or a decision about which company sees your writing. QUILL runs its own AI service, it is free, and it is the first thing in the AI menu (the &AI menu, so Alt then A opens it).

What the AI menu offers

Key Command What it does
Ctrl+Alt+G Free AI Assistant… Summarise, rewrite, proofread, shorten or explain the passage you are in
Ctrl+Alt+Z Ask About This Document… Ask a question about what you are writing
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F2 Free AI Usage… What you have used and what is left
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F4 Connect or Sign Out… Connect this computer, or disconnect it
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K Privacy Agreement… Read what is sent, and accept or withdraw
Alt+F2 Use My Own AI Key… Every limit lifted, billed to your OpenAI or Google Gemini account
Alt+F5 Use My ChatGPT Subscription… Every AI command on the ChatGPT plan you already pay for
Ctrl+F5 Ask About an Image… A picture described, on your ChatGPT subscription
Ctrl+F3 Tidy Dictated Text… Dictation’s misheard words and punctuation corrected, nothing else changed
Ctrl+F10 Dictionary > Word Explorer… Everything about the word you are on, as used in this sentence
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+' Dictionary > Define in Context What the word means here, and what you might be confusing it with
Ctrl+Shift+; Dictionary > Synonyms That Fit Replacements that keep the sentence’s meaning, already in the right form
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+] Dictionary > Find the Word For… The reverse dictionary: describe the meaning, get the word

The first five are the same five commands QUILL Lite has, so anything you learn in one editor you have learned in both. Three of the five keys are the same as well. Usage and Connect differ: in QUILL, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F7 to F12 open the other QuillVille apps, so QUILL uses F2 and F4 for those two, while QUILL Lite, which has no apps to open, uses Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9 and F10.

What it works on

The free AI works on the selection. With nothing selected it takes the paragraph you are in, or else the section. It never sends the whole file.

Nothing is applied without a keystroke from you. Every answer arrives in a window with Replace and Insert buttons, and both go through the ordinary undo list. If you typed over the text while the answer was on its way, Replace is not offered, and QUILL tells you so instead of writing the answer somewhere it does not belong.

You never wait for it, either. Requests run in the background, so you can keep typing, save, switch documents or close the window while an answer is coming.

QUILLBee’s tip: Changed your mind about an AI edit? Press Ctrl+Z. It comes back out exactly like anything else you typed.

The Free AI Assistant pad (Ctrl+Alt+G)

The pad has a list called What do you want done? with seventeen choices. Press a letter in the list to jump.

  • The four basics: Summarize, Rewrite, Proofread and Explain.
  • Ten writing tools: Shorten, Simplify, Make more formal, Make friendlier, Turn into a list, Find action items, Suggest headings, Continue writing, Write an email reply and Translate. When you choose Translate, a Translate into list appears with twenty languages.
  • Three that need you to type: Ask a question about the document, Ask a general question, and Have a conversation.

Every one of them is a single request of the same size, so the writing tools cost no more of your allowance than Summarize.

Having a conversation

Choose Have a conversation in the pad, or press Follow Up in any answer window, and the AI Conversation window opens. Here you can talk back and forth, and each reply remembers what was said before.

  1. Focus is in Your message. Type, then press Enter.
  2. Each reply is read aloud as it arrives and added to the Conversation above. Press Shift+Tab to reach it.
  3. Beside Send are Copy Last Reply, Insert Last Reply Below and New Conversation.

If you started with a question about the document, each follow-up keeps sending the same passages, so you can keep asking about them.

On the free AI each message counts as one request, and conversations have a monthly share of 40 of your 100 requests. The conversation so far goes with each message only as far as the ordinary size limit allows, so no message costs more than any other, and a long conversation slowly forgets its beginning. The window tells you the first time that happens. With your own OpenAI or Gemini key there is no such limit: the whole conversation goes, billed to your account.

There is a monthly, a daily and an hourly allowance, and a smaller one for a computer’s first 48 hours. Free AI limits, later in this chapter, has every number and every rule.

Nothing is sent until you ask

The free AI makes no request when QUILL starts, while you type, when you save, when you are idle or when focus moves. If you leave it switched on and never use it, QUILL makes no network call for it at all.

The first time you reach for it, QUILL shows you exactly what is sent and what is kept, and nothing leaves your computer until you accept. You can come to that same agreement three ways: AI > Privacy Agreement… (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K), Preferences, and Customize Features. All three show the same answer, so they never disagree.

If you withdraw, QUILL signs this computer out of the free AI as well, so no sign-in is left behind for a service you have said no to. QUILL remembers which version of the agreement you accepted (the setting ai_privacy_accepted_version), so if what is sent ever changes in an important way, you are asked again.

Basic and Advanced menus

The AI menu starts out Basic. It shows the five free AI commands above, the Use Artificial Intelligence switch, and Show advanced AI features. Basic is for everybody who just wants a paragraph tidied up.

The full menu has much more: provider setup, Ask Quill, the agents, Proofread, Transform, Translate, Read Aloud, Transcribe, More, the AI Library and the AI Hub. It is worth having once you have chosen which company should see your writing and have a key to paste in.

Nothing is taken away in Basic. Every advanced command keeps its keyboard shortcut and stays in the Command Palette; Basic only changes what the menu offers. Check Show advanced AI features near the bottom of the AI menu and everything comes back at once. QUILL remembers your choice.

If you already had AI set up when you updated (you had run the wizard, or saved a provider key), QUILL leaves you in Advanced, so no menu you were using disappears.

Setting up AI with the wizard

The first item in the AI menu is Set Up AI…, labelled “start here” until you have used it. It is a short wizard that gets you to working AI in a minute, in plain words.

  1. Welcome. A short note on what QUILL’s AI does, and that it is optional, shown to you before anything changes, and private by default.
  2. How would you like AI to run? Pick one:
    • On your device with Ollama. Private and free. It runs on your computer with no account or key, and QUILL connects to Ollama installed there.
    • Use an AI account. The most capable models. Connect Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter or Ollama Cloud with a key you paste once, which QUILL stores safely on this computer.
    • Not right now. AI stays off, and you can set it up any time later.
  3. Connect. For an account, pick a provider, paste your key, and press Test connection before you go on. For on-device AI, QUILL points itself at Ollama.
  4. You’re all set. A short summary of what you can now do, and a Keep it simple checkbox that turns on Basic mode.

QUILL also offers the wizard when you reach for AI before it is set up, for example when you ask for minutes from a transcript, so you never hit a dead end. Run Set Up AI again whenever you want to change provider or mode.

Basic mode is the default on a new install, and it hides the whole advanced menu, not just the agents. The wizard’s Keep it simple checkbox turns it on, and Show advanced AI features turns it off.

Using AI for free

You never have to pay to use AI in QUILL. Besides QUILL’s own free AI, the Connect step of the wizard recommends two free paths and picks good settings for you.

  • Most private, free. Pick Ollama (on your device). A model runs on your own computer: no account, no key, it works offline, and nothing you write leaves your machine. The quality is more modest than the big cloud models. If Ollama is not installed yet, do not install it by hand. AI > Set Up Local AI (Ollama)… does the whole job: it reports your computer’s memory, graphics card and free disk space, downloads and starts the official installer, downloads a model that suits your computer, and connects QUILL to it. Each step tells you what to do next, and it never moves on without you.
  • Best quality, free. Pick OpenRouter. Choose Get API key to open OpenRouter’s key page in your browser, create a free key and paste it back. QUILL picks a strong free writing model for you (at the moment a free Llama 3.3 70B model). The model’s description says Free, so you always know a choice costs nothing.

Every provider that needs a key has a Get API key button beside the key box that opens the right sign-up page.

A few honest notes:

  • Free cloud models can be slower and are rate-limited. Because the key is your own, that limit is yours alone; nobody else shares it, and it costs nobody anything.
  • Free hosted models may keep or train on what you send, under their own terms. If your writing is confidential, use the private on-device option.
  • What works on free models: everyday help works well, such as Rewrite, Summarize, Expand, Continue, Fix Grammar, Table of Contents, translating and proofreading. Ask Quill works too; on a small model it keeps its steps simple so it answers instead of stalling. The longest multi-step agent tasks are where a stronger paid model still does better. QUILL tells you when a task would benefit from one, but never stops you trying on a free model.
  • QUILL tidies on-device answers for you. Small on-device models have a few habits. When you use Rewrite, Summarize, Expand, Continue or Shorten on the on-device model, QUILL gives the model worked examples first, then checks the answer for hedging (“it seems”, “arguably”), editorialising (“clearly”, “obviously”) and filler openings (“In today’s world”, “It is important to note”), and tries once more to remove them. Fix Grammar and Improve Reading Order are left alone, so your own wording is never changed. This happens only on the on-device model; cloud answers are left as they come.

You can change your provider or model any time from Set Up AI or the AI Hub.

AI Assistant

Beyond the free AI, QUILL has a full AI assistant. You can run it on your own computer (llama.cpp with a local GGUF model) or connect a provider: Ollama (local), Ollama Cloud, OpenAI, Claude, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, or a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Every provider is optional, and you choose it yourself. Keys are kept in the Windows Credential Manager, with a DPAPI-encrypted file as a fallback, and are never written to disk as plain text. Where your keys are kept, later in this chapter, has the details.

Setting up an AI provider

Open AI > AI Hub… to set up your providers. The AI Hub is the one place for every provider’s key, model, Test Chat and key removal. If you are looking for the old AI Model and Connection or Forget API Key menu items, they are part of the AI Hub now.

  • OpenRouter. Paste your key into the OpenRouter API Key field. One OpenRouter key reaches many models, including Claude, GPT-4o and Gemini.
  • OpenAI. Paste your OpenAI API key.
  • Ollama. No key needed. Install Ollama on your computer (ollama serve) and QUILL finds it by itself at http://localhost:11434. If you run Ollama on a different port or computer, change the Ollama Base URL setting.

You can also set a Default model for prompt runs (ai_prompt_default_model). Leave it blank and Ask AI and the Prompt Library use the same model, or name a more capable model here for prompt library work.

Ask Quill (Alt+Q) and Ask AI

AI > Ask Quill… (Alt+Q) opens the assistant as a conversation. You can ask questions, draft text, suggest edits, and run QUILL commands, and nothing changes until you approve it. The window shows the provider and model in use, and you can switch either one there.

When you only want a quick answer, with nothing to insert and no follow-up, use AI > Ask AI… from the Command Palette. It is a simple question and answer window.

  1. Provider and Model already hold the last ones you used. If they are set up, focus goes straight to the Prompt field so you can start typing. If not, focus starts on Provider so you can set it up.
  2. Type your question and press Ctrl+Enter, or the Send button. QUILL says “Sending…” and the button is unavailable until the answer arrives.
  3. The answer opens in a read-only window. Read it with the arrow keys, and use Copy to Clipboard to copy all of it. Closing the answer brings you back to Ask AI, ready for a follow-up.

Clear empties the prompt field and puts you back in it.

Check Grammar with AI

Edit > Grammar > Check Grammar with AI sends the selected text, or the whole document if nothing is selected, to your AI model and asks it to review the grammar. The answer lists each correction as the original phrase, the corrected phrase and the reason. Nothing is changed for you; you make the corrections yourself.

Out of the box, the model is told to list only the corrections needed and not to rewrite the passage. To give it different instructions, open the Prompt Library, find the built-in “Check Grammar” prompt and edit its text. The command uses your version from then on.

Free AI limits, and when they start again

QUILL’s free AI is free because everybody shares it, so it has limits. Here is every one of them in one place. Free AI Usage (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F2) shows where you stand.

Your allowance at a glance

These are the service’s current settings. QUILL reads them from the service each time, so they can change without an update, and Usage always shows the numbers that apply to you right now.

Limit How many Starts again
Requests a month 100 The 1st of the month
Requests a day 20 Every night
Requests an hour 8 At the top of each hour
Any one kind of request a month 60 The 1st of the month
A new connection’s first 48 hours 15 Rises to 100 on its own

“Any one kind” means Summarize, Rewrite, Proofread, Explain and Ask About This Document each have a monthly share of 60, so no single one can use up the whole month. The daily and hourly limits are there to stop something running away with a month’s worth in an afternoon. Ordinary work rarely comes near them.

When the counts start again

The service keeps time in UTC, not your own time zone.

  • The hour starts again on the hour.
  • The day starts again at midnight UTC. That is 8 PM Eastern or 5 PM Pacific in summer, an hour earlier in winter, so in North America the new day’s requests arrive in the evening.
  • The month starts again at midnight UTC on the 1st. Usage shows the exact date.

What counts as a request

One request is one press of Send that comes back with an answer. Try Again is another request. A request that brings no answer is not counted: if it was too long, if there was no connection, if the service had a problem, or if you had already reached a limit, nothing is used. Opening Usage or About never uses anything.

When you reach a limit

The AI window tells you which limit you reached and when it starts again, and focus moves to that message so you can read it again with the arrow keys. It ends with an error code, QUILL-AI-GATEWAY-QUOTA for a limit, which is worth including if you write to support. Nothing is used, nothing in your document changes, and the rest of QUILL carries on as normal. Wait until the time it gives you, or ask for more (see Asking for more, below).

If the message says QUILL’s free AI is paused, it is not about you. The service has one spending ceiling for everybody together, and when that is reached the free AI pauses for everyone until the 1st. This is rare, and QUILL tells you when it happens.

A new connection starts smaller

For its first 48 hours, a computer that has just connected gets 15 requests, and then the full allowance starts on its own. You do not need to do anything. It stops somebody connecting over and over for a fresh allowance each time, and someone trying the free AI out rarely uses 15 on the first day. While it applies, Usage and About say so and tell you exactly when it ends. Signing out and connecting again starts a new connection, so it never gets you more.

Computers that share an internet connection

A household, a classroom or a library usually reaches the internet through one address, and a few limits apply to that address as a whole: how many computers can be connected from it at once, how many new connections it can make in an hour, and a monthly total shared by every computer on it. They are generous for a home. The exact numbers are not published, so that nobody can use them to make connections by the hundred. Signing a computer out gives its place back.

If a class or a lab runs into these limits, write to support. Helping with exactly this is part of their job.

Asking for more

Choose Get Help from Support in the Help menu, and say what you need and why: a course, a deadline, a book. When this computer is connected, its support ID goes into the message by itself, and that is all support needs to find you; there is no account name or password to give. Support can raise your monthly allowance, and can end the new-connection allowance early. The change applies from your next request. You do not need to sign out, reconnect or update, and Usage shows the new number the next time you open it.

Your support ID is also in Help > About and in Usage, with a Copy Support ID button, if you would rather write from somewhere else.

Using your own OpenAI or Google Gemini key

If you have an OpenAI account or a Google Gemini key, you can use your own key instead of QUILL’s free service, and every limit goes away: no monthly, daily or hourly allowance, no 2,250-word ceiling, and no smaller first 48 hours.

Setting up your key (Alt+F2)

AI > Use My Own AI Key… (Alt+F2) opens one window. Its parts, in Tab order:

  • Provider. OpenAI or Google Gemini. Everything else in the window follows this choice: where your text goes, which key, which models and whose prices. AI help uses the key saved for the provider you choose here, never the other one. The choice is saved with your settings (ai_own_key_provider), and QUILL never guesses it from a key or a model name.
  • About this. A read-only box that says exactly where your text goes. Arrow through it once.
  • API key. Paste the key for the provider you chose. An OpenAI key comes from platform.openai.com, under API keys, and starts with sk-. A Gemini key comes from Google AI Studio at aistudio.google.com/apikey.
  • Model. Every model your key can use for text, filled in from your account once the key is checked. For OpenAI, Luna 6 first, then the other GPT-6 models; for Gemini, 2.5 Flash first, then 2.5 Pro; then the rest by name. Each row says roughly what it costs, for example “gpt-6-luna, about $0.57 per 100 requests (estimate)”, so arrowing down the list is enough to compare them. Your choice is saved as ai_own_key_model. Models that cannot answer in text (speech, transcription, images, embeddings) are left out.
  • Cost estimate. The chosen model’s estimated cost per request and per 100 requests, at that provider’s prices. These are estimates to help you compare, not the provider’s prices. A typical request is about a page in and a paragraph back. The real prices are at openai.com/api/pricing and ai.google.dev/pricing.
  • Status. Whether a key is saved for the chosen provider, what the last test said, and whether a key for the other provider is saved too.
  • Test the Key. Checks the key with your provider, fills the model list, then sends one tiny request to the chosen model and tells you whether it answered. That request costs a fraction of a cent.
  • Remove the Saved Key. Forgets the chosen provider’s key at once and puts AI help straight back on QUILL’s free service.

Press OK and the key is saved. QUILL says “AI help uses your own OpenAI key, with no limits”, or names your own Google Gemini key.

To change the model later, press Alt+F2. With a key saved, the list of models is there straight away. Pick another and press OK.

There is no separate switch to find. While a key is saved for the chosen provider, AI help uses it. Remove the key and AI help goes back to the free service, with its free allowance, at that moment.

You can save both keys. The Provider list decides which one is used. With OpenAI chosen, a saved Gemini key just waits; the Status line tells you it is there, and choosing Google Gemini puts it to work. QUILL never decides from which key exists or from a model’s name, so a request never goes to a company you did not choose.

With a Gemini key, Ask About an Image works too. Gemini’s models can read pictures, which the free service and an OpenAI key here cannot, so Ctrl+F5 answers on a Gemini key just as it does on a ChatGPT subscription.

What changes with your own key

  • Your text goes straight from this computer to the provider you chose, OpenAI or Google, on your account. Nothing passes through QUILL’s servers, so QUILL records nothing at all, not even the count it keeps for the free service.
  • OpenAI or Google bills you for each request, under that company’s own terms and privacy policy.
  • Usage (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F2) opens a different window. It tells you which model is answering and that no allowance applies, and its Open My Usage button takes you to the usage page of your OpenAI or Google AI Studio account, where your requests and charges are. There is no Sign Out and no support ID in it, because neither applies. Help > About also shows the model and that page’s address instead of the free allowance.
  • You do not need to connect this computer, and you are not asked to accept the free service’s agreement, which covers QUILL’s servers. Your own key never touches them.
  • The pad, what it can do, and what comes back are the same, down to the instructions sent with your text.
  • There are no limits. Nothing is refused for being too long, the answer is not cut short, and Ask a question about the document sends the whole document instead of the three passages that match best, so nothing is missed.
  • You get warnings instead of limits. The About to send line tells you how many words are going and roughly what they cost with the model you chose (an estimate, not your provider’s bill), and that the answer costs extra. It also tells you when the text is more than the free service would accept, and, for something very large, that it may be more than the model can read at once. In that case the provider refuses it and charges nothing.

Where your own key is kept

In Windows’ own credential store, not a settings file. Once saved it is never shown again: the box stays empty and says a key is saved. A portable copy of QUILL keeps it in an encrypted file instead. QUILL and QUILL Lite share the key, so a key saved in either works in both, and removing it in either removes it from both.

If a request fails

You hear why, followed by the error code QUILL-AI-OWN-KEY-FAILED, and the message names the provider. The usual causes are a mistyped key, a model your account cannot use, an account with no credit, or the wrong provider chosen for the key you saved. Test the Key tells you which.

Using your ChatGPT subscription

If you already pay for ChatGPT, AI > Use My ChatGPT Subscription… (Alt+F5) runs every free AI command on that plan instead. There is no key to paste and no bill per request.

  1. Press Alt+F5, then press Continue with ChatGPT.
  2. Your browser opens on OpenAI’s own sign-in page. Allow “QUILL” to use your plan.
  3. Come back to QUILL. You are signed in.

From then on the pad, its seventeen choices, Ask About This Document and conversations go straight from this computer to OpenAI on your plan, with no monthly allowance, no size limit, no charge per request, and nothing through QUILL’s servers.

Once you are signed in, the window offers:

  • Model. Your plan’s own models, read from your account. The first is chosen for you, and whichever you arrow to is saved.
  • Allow web search. Off until you check it. When it is on, the model may search the web through OpenAI to answer a question.
  • Open ChatGPT Usage. Your plan’s own page, which shows its limits and what is left.
  • Sign Out. Two presses. It asks OpenAI to cancel QUILL’s sign-in and forgets it here.
  • Forget on This Computer. Forgets the sign-in here only.

Sign Out and Forget on This Computer are only there while you are signed in.

How the sign-in works

Each QuillVille app signs in on its own. QUILL’s sign-in is not QUILL Lite’s, QUILL Cast’s or Quill Radio’s; each appears under its own name in Apps in ChatGPT’s settings, and signing out of one leaves the others signed in. When another app is already signed in on this computer, the Status line says so, because your browser is then signed in already and Continue with ChatGPT is a single Allow instead of a password.

A ChatGPT sign-in is used ahead of a saved OpenAI key, since the plan is already paid for and a key is billed per request. It needs neither the free service’s connection nor its agreement, which covers QUILL’s servers. QUILL keeps only a refresh token, in Windows’ credential store, under QUILL’s own name. Usage opens this window when you are on a plan, and About names the account and the model.

When something goes wrong, the message carries a code and tells you what to do next: QUILL-AI-CHATGPT-SIGNED-OUT (sign in again), -LIMIT (you have used the plan’s allowance for now), -UNAVAILABLE, -SIGNIN or -FAILED.

Ask About an Image (Ctrl+F5)

This is the one AI command that works on a file. Choose a JPEG, PNG, WebP or GIF picture, ask a question about it or none, and hear what the model sees: a description written for a blind reader, with any text in the picture copied out exactly. The answer opens in an Image Description window with Insert Below and Copy, and Ctrl+Z takes an insert back. It needs your ChatGPT subscription (or, as above, your own Gemini key); without one it says so and opens the account window.

Tidy Dictated Text (Ctrl+F3)

This is the AI for dictation. The selection, or else the paragraph at the cursor, goes to the model with an instruction to correct what speech recognition got wrong (sound-alike words, names, words run together, punctuation, capitals, fillers and false starts) and to change nothing else. The Tidied Dictation window offers Replace My Selection, and Ctrl+Z takes it back in one step. It runs on a ChatGPT subscription or your own OpenAI key, and never on the free allowance. With neither, it says so and opens the account window.

My Dictation Instructions

You can tell Tidy Dictated Text how you like your writing. Open Dictation Settings (Alt+Shift+F6), press More Dictation Settings… (Alt+A), then My Dictation Instructions… (Alt+I). A short file opens in QUILL. Write one instruction per line, in plain words, and save it:

  • Write numbers as digits.
  • Use British spelling.
  • QUILL is always written in capitals.
  • Never change legal terms.

From then on, Tidy Dictated Text follows them. They go with the passage you tidy, and only then: never with every phrase as you talk. The AI is told that your dictated text is something to correct, never a request to answer, so “ask Sam to send the report” comes back tidied, not answered.

The Dictionary submenu

The Dictionary submenu of the AI menu is a dictionary that reads the sentence. It asks thirteen questions about the word you are on. Each sends the word and the sentence it sits in, never the rest of the document, and the answer is written to be listened to. Where it helps, you also get a list of choices, each saying why.

  • Define in Context (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+')
  • Synonyms That Fit (Ctrl+Shift+;)
  • Simpler Word (Ctrl+Shift+-)
  • More Formal Word (Ctrl+Shift+=)
  • More Vivid Word (Ctrl+Shift+')
  • Opposites (Alt+Shift+-)
  • Is This the Right Word? (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+/)
  • Use It in a Sentence (Alt+Shift+=)
  • Where It Comes From (Alt+Shift+,)
  • How to Say It (Alt+Shift+')
  • Rhymes (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+;)
  • Word Explorer (Ctrl+F10), which answers all of them at once
  • Find the Word For… (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+]), the reverse dictionary

The same items are in the Dictionary for “word” submenu when you press the Applications key on a word. The answer window opens on the answer. Press Tab to reach the Choices, then Enter or Use This Word replaces the word as one undo step (Find the Word For inserts at the cursor instead). It only does so while the word is still where it was.

Like Tidy Dictated Text, the dictionary runs only on a ChatGPT subscription or your own OpenAI key. A dictionary gets asked a hundred times a day, and that would spend a free allowance on synonyms. With neither, it says so and opens the account window. QUILL Lite has the same thirteen items on the same keys.

Where your keys are kept

Portable mode and key storage

Normally QUILL keeps AI provider keys in the Windows Credential Manager, which ties them to your Windows user account. If you run QUILL from a self-contained folder, for example on a network share or a USB drive, portable mode keeps all your keys in that folder with the rest of your QUILL data.

Turning on portable mode

The portable bundle comes with an empty data\ folder next to quill.exe, and that folder is what tells QUILL to run portable. There is nothing to set: just run quill.exe from the bundle’s main folder. The Setup Wizard’s Data location page notices the portable install and offers the portable choice for you. To turn an installed copy into a portable one, copy the install folder to a USB drive and make an empty data\ folder at its top level; QUILL switches to portable mode the next time it starts from there.

If you used to set QUILL_PORTABLE=1, you no longer need to; QUILL ignores it now, and the data\ folder is what counts.

Nothing is written to the computer you plug into. Extract the zip, run quill.exe, and your settings, keymap and everything else go straight into the data\ folder beside it. No folder appears in %APPDATA% on that computer.

If you ran a portable QUILL before version 1.0 and your settings look as if they have reset, they have not. Older portable copies kept them in %APPDATA%\Quill on that computer. Copy that folder’s contents into the bundle’s data\ folder to bring them across.

You can still choose otherwise. Picking Windows profile in Preferences or the Setup Wizard is remembered and wins over the bundle, because a choice you make yourself always beats a default. The same goes for every QuillVille app with a portable build: Quill Radio, QUILL Cast, Quill Weather, Audio Studio, Converter, Inkwell, Beacon, Media Player and QUILL Lite.

Keys in portable mode

In portable mode, keys are kept in a file called keys.enc in the QUILL data folder. It is encrypted with Windows DPAPI, so it is protected by your Windows user account.

The encrypted file only opens for the Windows account that made it. Copy it to another computer or another Windows account and it cannot be read, so you will need to type your keys in again there. Portable mode gives you a self-contained folder on one computer; it does not carry your keys from one computer to another.

How QUILL protects your keys and sign-ins

Everything secret QUILL holds for you (AI provider keys, remote site passwords, and the sign-in tokens for any online service you connect) goes into one protected store. On Windows that is the Windows Credential Manager, or the DPAPI-encrypted keys.enc file in portable mode; on macOS it is the login Keychain. QUILL never writes a secret as plain text, and never puts one in a settings file, a log, a diagnostic bundle or its own program files.

When you sign out of a service, QUILL clears every secret that service stored, in one step, so nothing is left behind. No secret is ever part of QUILL itself, so there is nothing to dig out of the program: your keys and tokens live only in your operating system’s protected store, tied to your account. If QUILL ever adds a sign-in for another service, such as an online library, its tokens will be kept there too.

Keys from environment variables

For developers and test machines, keys can also come from environment variables, whichever storage mode is on. These always win and are never saved to disk.

Provider Environment variable
OpenRouter QUILL_OPENROUTER_KEY
OpenAI QUILL_OPENAI_KEY
Ollama Cloud QUILL_OLLAMA_KEY
AI Assistant QUILL_ASSISTANT_KEY

The AI Library

AI > AI Library… is the one home for everything QUILL can do with AI on your writing. It has three tabs, all with the same buttons (Run, Edit, Enable/Disable, Import, Export):

  • Prompts. Single instructions you run on the selection or document, such as “Rewrite warmly” or “Summarize”. New, Edit, Delete, and Promote a prompt into a Skill.
  • Skills. Workflows of several steps, saved as .sqp packs you can share. Run, Import, Export and Remove them, and Promote a Skill into an Agent.
  • Agents. The catalogue of agents that can use tools (Writing Companion, Reviewer, Code Doctor and more), plus any you have saved yourself. Run them through the reviewed gateway, or Validate one against the agent standard.

The three grow into one another. Promote turns a Prompt into a Skill and a Skill into an Agent, so you can start simple and add power when you need it. Anything you build is yours to Export and share, and a friend or colleague can Import it.

Build an AI Action

On the Skills tab, Build Action… opens a simple form. It is the easiest way to teach QUILL something new, and there is no syntax to learn.

  1. Name your action, for example “My Monday standup notes”.
  2. Start from a built-in example (Meeting Minutes, Action Items and the rest) or a blank page. An example fills in the instructions for you to adjust.
  3. Describe what you want in plain language. That is all the “programming” there is: no Markdown, no metadata, no syntax.
  4. Attach a reference if you like: an agenda, your house style, or an earlier example you were happy with. QUILL matches its format and wording, as in “Make minutes that look like last month’s.”
  5. Save. Your action becomes a real Skill in the Library, ready to Run on any document, change later, Promote to an Agent, or share.

Prompt Library

AI > Prompt Library… opens the full prompt manager.

On the left is a list of every prompt; type in the search field to filter it by name or category. On the right is the selected prompt’s instructions, and an optional input field where you can type or paste text to use instead of the selection.

To run a prompt:

  1. Select a prompt in the list, or type in the search field to find it.
  2. If you like, paste text into the input field. Left blank, QUILL uses the selection in the editor, or the whole document.
  3. Press Run with AI. The result opens in the AI Response window.
Built-in prompts

QUILL comes with eighteen prompts you can use straight away or as starting points:

  • Editing and tone: Check Grammar, Fix Grammar, Improve Clarity, Make Concise, Active Voice, Formal Tone, Conversational Tone, Paraphrase.
  • Structure: Summarize, Convert to Bullet Points, Generate FAQs, Step-by-Step Instructions.
  • Writing: Continue from Here, Draft a Speech, Summary Email, Social Media Post (280 characters or fewer).
  • Research: Define This Term, Find Counterarguments.

The ones in bold are the newer one-shot tools.

Built-in prompts are always there. You can change their wording or disable them, but you cannot delete them.

Managing prompts
  • New Prompt. A small window: type a name, choose a category, and write the instructions. Put {selection} where you want QUILL to insert the text.
  • Edit. Change the name, category or instructions of a prompt you made. For a built-in prompt you can change its text; your version is saved and the original is kept.
  • Disable/Enable. Hides or shows a prompt in the list without deleting it. Handy for built-ins you never use.
  • Delete. Removes a prompt you made. Built-in prompts cannot be deleted.
Prompts from Quillins

Quillins can add prompts to the library with a prompts.json file. The bundled ai-writing-prompts Quillin adds 7 more: Expand This, Vary Sentence Rhythm, Make More Vivid, Write a Title, Generate Outline, Suggest Supporting Evidence and Plain Language. They appear in the list and run like any other prompt, but they are not saved into your own library file.

Sharing prompt packs

QUILL shares prompt collections as .pqp (Prompt Quill Pack) files.

  • Import .pqp. Choose a file, and every prompt in it is added. Prompts whose names are already in your library are skipped.
  • Export .pqp. Saves all the prompts you have made to a .pqp file you can share or keep as a backup.

A .pqp file is plain JSON that is easy to read:

{
  "schema": "quill.prompt-pack/1",
  "name": "My Writing Prompts",
  "prompts": [
    {
      "name": "Make Punchy",
      "text": "Rewrite this as a punchy one-liner: {selection}",
      "category": "Editing"
    }
  ]
}

Skill Library

A prompt is one instruction. A skill is a series of steps, and each step can use what the step before it produced.

AI > Skill Library… opens the Skill Library.

A skill has a name, a description and a list of steps. If the skill asks for choices, such as tone, reading level or kind of output, QUILL asks you for them before it runs. Each step then sends its prompt to the AI in turn and hands the answer on to the next step.

Bundled skills

Four skills come with QUILL, in the ai-writing-skills Quillin:

  • Accessible Rewrite. Looks for plain-language problems in your text (long sentences, passive voice, jargon), then rewrites it for the reading level you choose: Grade 6, 8 or 10. The rewrite replaces the selection when you Accept.
  • Research and Draft. Finds the main topic of your selection, gathers five supporting facts, then drafts a paragraph in the tone and length you choose.
  • Meeting Notes to Action Items. Reads meeting notes, pulls out every action item with its owner and deadline, checks for any it missed, and writes a clean follow-up summary. The result goes to the clipboard.
  • Argument Strengthener. Works out how your argument fits together, finds its weak points and the counterarguments, then writes a stronger version for the audience you choose.
Running a skill
  1. Open AI > Skill Library….
  2. Select a skill in the list.
  3. Press Run. If the skill needs choices, a small window appears; fill them in and press OK.
  4. QUILL says “Running step 1 of N…” as each step starts.
  5. When it finishes, the result window appears. Read it, then press Accept to put it in your document (for skills that do that), or Copy to copy it to the clipboard.

Each step waits for the whole answer before the next one starts, instead of showing it word by word. That keeps every step’s result complete and easy to read.

Writing and sharing skills

A skill is a .sqp (Skill Quill Pack) file: a plain Markdown document with YAML front matter at the top. Open any .sqp file in QUILL to read and edit it, and share a skill by sharing the file. The appendix on writing skills, at the end of this guide, walks you through it, and the full reference is section 20 of docs/quillins.md.

To check a skill file for mistakes before you share it, run:

python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator yourskill.sqp

The rest of the AI menu

Once Show advanced AI features is checked, the AI menu holds everything QUILL’s assistant can do. Here are the parts this chapter has not covered yet.

Quick writing actions

AI > Transform Selection has the small writing chores, so they never pull you out of the editor: Rewrite Selection, Summarize Selection, Expand Selection, Continue Writing, Fix Grammar and Generate Table of Contents.

Rewrite Selection, Summarize Selection, Continue Writing and Fix Grammar work with or without a selection:

  • Rewrite Selection and Fix Grammar act on your selection if you have one. Otherwise they use the paragraph at the cursor.
  • Summarize Selection acts on your selection if you have one. Otherwise it summarizes the whole document.
  • Continue Writing uses your selection as the lead-in if you have one. Otherwise it continues from the full document.

QUILL tells you the scope it chose before anything happens, for example “Rewrite paragraph (42 words)”, so you always know what the action will change. If there is nothing to act on, QUILL says so (“Nothing to rewrite”) and sends nothing. If AI is turned off, these actions say “AI is turned off. Enable ‘Use Artificial Intelligence’ in the AI menu.” and do nothing else.

On the on-device model, Summarize works in two passes. The first pulls the plain observations out of your text. The second writes a short summary from those observations, to a word budget, with the original out of view. This keeps a small local model much closer to what your text actually says, so it does not invent its own interpretation. Cloud providers do it in a single pass, because they do not need the help.

Rewrite & Improve Selection

AI > Rewrite & Improve Selection changes with the kind of document you are in, so it only offers what makes sense there. In ordinary writing it has Rewrite clearly, Shorten, Make warmer, Review and Check accessibility. In a code file it offers jobs for code instead. Select the text first and choose one. The rewritten text takes the place of your selection, and Ctrl+Z puts the original back if you prefer it.

Run Agent

An agent is a helper with one job and the skills for it. AI > Run Agent lists every agent QUILL has: Accessibility Editor, Citation & Link Fixer, Code Doctor, Data Cleaner, GitHub Maintainer, Markdown Publisher, Math Tutor, Meeting Notes to Action Items, Plain-Language Rewriter, PRD Architect, QUILL Concierge, Release Notes Builder, Researcher, Reviewer, Summarizer and Writing Companion. Choose one and it works on your selection or your document, whichever it was made for. One that changes your selection does it in place. One that changes the whole document shows you a preview first, and nothing changes until you accept it. One that only reports opens what it found in a new document.

Agents can only use a short, safe list of editing tools, and they still need AI turned on. In Safe Mode, or with AI off, the items stay on the menu but tell you why they cannot run. The AI Library, below, is where you look at an agent more closely, or make your own.

Your writing instructions

AI > More > Writing Instructions… opens a short document of rules the assistant always follows when it writes for you: who you are writing for, the tone you like, words you never want to see. The first time, QUILL starts it for you with those three headings to fill in. It is an ordinary document, so edit it however you like and save it. The assistant reads it again every time it writes, so a change counts straight away.

Writing Assistant, Prompt Studio and Agent Center

These three older windows are no longer on the menu, because the AI Library now does their jobs in one place. You can still reach them by name from the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P):

  • Writing Assistant finds the QUILL commands that match what you type, and offers ready-made prompts for rewriting, summarizing, continuing and fixing grammar. It is also where Ask Quill Chat lives, described in the next topic.
  • Prompt Studio lets you build your own reusable prompts with template variables.
  • Agent Center writes a guided plan for a task. You review the plan before sending it to the Writing Assistant.

Run Python

Run Python…, a button in the Writing Assistant, runs a small piece of restricted Python against the current document text and selection, so you can transform text in ways no menu command offers. The restriction is a list of allowed imports and some limits on time and memory. It is not a security boundary. Only run Python code you trust or wrote yourself.

Connecting to an AI provider

The quickest way in is the AI Hub (AI > AI Hub…), one place that links provider checks, model lists, Prompt Studio, Agent Center and the Writing Assistant. The AI Hub topic below walks through it in full. In short:

  1. Open AI Hub and choose a provider: Ollama (local), Ollama Cloud, OpenAI, Claude, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, or Custom OpenAI-compatible.
  2. Confirm the host URL and model.
  3. Enter a key only if your endpoint needs one.
  4. Use Verify Connection to test the endpoint and your key.
  5. Use List Models to fetch the endpoint’s models, then type in the search box to narrow the list.
  6. Use Recommend Model to pick a model that suits your computer and the kind of work you do.
  7. Save. QUILL checks the connection on its own and updates the AI status line in the AI menu.

Most cloud providers come with their host URL already filled in, so setup is mostly about the key. For an unusual OpenAI-compatible endpoint, choose Custom and set the host and model yourself. With Google Gemini, a model you pick from the list QUILL fetches works as it is. Gemini names its models models/gemini-..., and QUILL drops that prefix for you.

QUILL keeps any key you enter in Windows Credential Manager, with a DPAPI-encrypted file as a fallback, and speaks the result of every check in plain words.

Connection status messages

Each message tells you what to do next:

  • “Authentication failed. Check your API key.” The key was rejected (HTTP 401). Enter it again.
  • “Access denied. Your API key is valid but lacks permission for this model or region.” The key works but is not allowed for that model, region or billing tier (HTTP 403). Check the provider’s model access, billing or quota.
  • “The AI provider is warming up. Try again in a moment.” The model is still loading. QUILL retries briefly on its own before telling you this.
  • “The local AI server is not running. Start Ollama and try again.” QUILL could not reach your local endpoint.
  • “Rate limited by the AI provider. Wait a moment and try again.” You sent requests too quickly.
  • “Your saved API key could not be unlocked on this device. Open AI Connection and enter the key again.” This shows in the AI status line when a saved key cannot be decrypted. It can happen after you move a portable copy of QUILL to a different Windows account or computer. Open AI Connection and enter the key again.

Trust and privacy baseline

  • The first time you run QUILL, it shows a trust and privacy consent acknowledgement.
  • QUILL does not keep AI chat transcripts by default.
