  • Complete Link or Tag… Start typing [[ (for a note) or # (for a tag), run this, and pick from a list that narrows as you type. QUILL inserts your choice and, for a link, adds the closing ]]. It does the job of a pop-up that appears as you type, but it speaks and holds focus.
  • Go to Note… jumps to a note. Start typing part of a title and the list narrows as you go, with QUILL speaking the count. Press Down to move into the list, or press Enter to open the closest match.
  • Search Vault… searches every note. Type a word or phrase and hear the number of results. Each result reads as its note title, line number, and the matching text. Turn on Regex for pattern searches, or Whole word to skip partial matches. Enter opens a result at its exact line.

Tags, embeds and templates

  • Show Tags… opens the tag pane. Filter your #tags (each shows a note count), open a tag, and get the list of notes that carry it. Nested tags roll up, so #area also finds notes tagged #area/sub.
  • Speak Embed at Cursor With the cursor on an ![[Other Note]] embed, hear the note (or the heading or block) it pulls in, without changing your text.
  • Resolve Embed Inline replaces that ![[embed]] with the actual content, as one change you can undo with Ctrl+Z.
  • Insert Template… Pick a template from a Templates folder inside your vault. QUILL fills in {{date}}, {{time}} and {{title}}, asks you out loud any {{prompt:Question}} it finds, inserts the result, and puts the cursor where you marked {{cursor}}.
  • Open Today’s Note, Previous Daily Note, Next Daily Note open today’s dated note (creating it if needed) and step back and forward through the days. Daily notes live at Journal/YYYY-MM-DD.md by default.

Sharing your vault

  • Export Vault as Website… Choose an output folder and QUILL writes a small website that needs nothing else: one accessible page per note, your [[links]] turned into real links between pages, your ![[embeds]] filled in, and an index page listing everything. It runs in the background and tells you how many pages it wrote.
  • Sync Vault If your vault folder is a Git repository with a remote you control, this commits your changes, pulls anyone else’s, and pushes, all in the background. If the same note changed in both places, QUILL lists the conflicts and stops instead of overwriting anything. It is disabled in Safe Mode. The same sync works on any folder, not just a vault; see QUILL Sync below.
  • Vault Settings… sets the folder your templates live in (default Templates) and the pattern for daily-note file names (default Journal/{{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}.md). Leave a box empty to keep the default.

How links work

Write a link by typing [[Note Title]] yourself, or use Insert Link to Note…. Links are plain text in your file, with nothing hidden, and they are resolved when you follow them, export, or build the website.

When you preview a note that lives in your vault, QUILL shows it resolved: [[links]] read as their titles, and ![[embeds]] filled in. Every time you save a note in the vault, its links, backlinks, tags and search results update straight away, with no need to reopen anything.

One Editor, Every Format

Every document opens in the same QUILL editor, and it has a real rich text mode. The thing to hold onto: bold means bold, and QUILL speaks your document’s language. The braille fix is on by default in every format; the braille troubleshooting entry in Chapter 11, Accessibility, speech and braille, has the details.

  • Writing Markdown (.md): Ctrl+B wraps your selection in **, and Insert Heading 2 puts ## at the start of the line.
  • Writing HTML (.html): Ctrl+B wraps in <strong>, and headings become real HTML headings.
  • Writing Rich Text (.rtf): the document opens formatted. Ctrl+B applies real bold, and Insert Heading 2 applies a real sized heading. The Format menu’s font, size, color, highlight and alignment commands change the actual formatting, and Describe Formatting at Cursor answers from the live document (“Arial, 14 point, bold, centered”). Search, spell check, read aloud, bookmarks, notes and braille all work as in any other document.
  • Writing plain text (.txt): text stays plain, because that is what a .txt file promises. The first time you press a formatting key, QUILL asks once: treat this document as Markdown, convert it to Rich Text, or stay plain. Your answer is remembered for that document.
  • Editing Word documents (.docx): a .docx can open for real rich editing and save back as a genuine Word file. If the file holds things QUILL’s editor cannot keep (images, comments, tracked changes, headers and footers), QUILL asks first. You can open it for reading and plain editing (the safe default), edit it as Rich Text with those losses named one by one, or edit a copy. The first rich save over such a file writes a timestamped backup next to it automatically. Tables are preserved when you open a Word document for rich editing: they appear inline as accessible tables, so you can read them and jump to them with single-key table navigation (T).

The Document Format switcher

Format > Document Format… moves the current document between Plain text, Markdown, HTML, Rich Text (RTF) and Word (.docx) while you work. You can also press Alt+Shift+F, use the command palette, or press Enter on the Format cell in the status bar, which always shows your current format.

Switching to a rich format turns your Markdown headings into real ones. Leaving a rich format warns you first, with a list of exactly what will not survive. A switched document never quietly overwrites its old file: the next save suggests the matching new name.

Every switch is a real conversion. Switching to HTML writes real HTML (<h1> and <strong>, not hashes and asterisks under an HTML label), and switching back reads it in again. Your formatting comes with you in every direction: headings, bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, superscript and subscript, font family and size, text colour and highlight, bullet and numbered lists, links, code spans and fences, block quotes, alignment, line spacing, indents, spacing before and after, named styles, page breaks, tables, images and horizontal rules. Switch out and back as often as you like; you end up with the document you started with.

Converting to Plain text asks you first. Plain text has no formatting, so there are two fair ways to handle Markdown already in your document, and QUILL won’t guess:

  • Remove the markers. # Heading becomes Heading, **bold** becomes bold, and the file is strictly plain.
  • Keep them as text. The # and ** stay as ordinary characters. A .txt file is allowed to contain them, and plenty of people keep their notes that way.

Escape (or Cancel) leaves the document alone. You are only asked when there is something to ask about; ordinary prose converts without a question.

If rich mode is unavailable

On a system where the bundled macOS bridge or the Windows COM bridge cannot load, .rtf and .docx documents open converted to editable text, the classic way, and save back through the same converters. Nothing is lost, and QUILL says so in the status bar. The Mac app includes everything rich mode needs; only source installs add it themselves (pip install "quill[mac]"). If you ever see the converted fallback on a normal install, please tell us through Help > Get Help from Support.

Table Studio (experimental)

Turn Table Studio on in the Experimental tab, and Tools > Table Studio… opens a table in a spreadsheet-style grid made for screen-reader users, instead of a wall of pipe characters. One grid does two jobs:

  • Table Studio starts a new table you build up cell by cell.
  • Open CSV in Table Studio opens a .csv or .tsv file straight into the grid. The delimiter is detected for you.

With Table Studio on, opening a .csv from File > Open and choosing the grid view brings it up in the same grid.

Moving and editing in the grid

The arrow keys move by cell. Up and Down change rows, and Left and Right move across columns and speak the column heading as you go, so you always know where you are.

  • Home and End jump to the first and last column.
  • Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End jump to the corners.
  • Page Up/Down move by ten rows.
  • F2 or Enter edits the active cell.
  • Alt+arrows move a whole row or column.
  • Ctrl+Insert adds a row.
  • Delete clears a cell.

The same actions are on buttons if you prefer them.

The table menu

Shift+F10 (or the Applications key, or right-click) opens a context menu with every table action in one place: Sort Ascending / Descending by the current column, Insert / Delete / Move rows, Insert / Delete columns, Rename Column Header, Promote First Row to Header (for a CSV whose header row was read as data), and Use First Column as Row Headers.

Headers are stored the standard way: <th scope="col"> and <th scope="row"> in HTML, and a proper header row in Markdown. That way screen readers and other tools understand your table’s structure.

Finishing a table

Insert as Markdown or Insert as HTML drops the finished table, with its headers, into your document. Save to CSV writes the grid back to a file, so a CSV you opened makes the full round trip.

NVDA and JAWS announce the column as you cross a row. Builds that include the optional native provider give richer cell announcements; without it QUILL uses a built-in fallback, and the feature works either way.

QUILL Sync

QUILL has no sync service of its own: no QUILL cloud account and no QUILL-hosted storage. To carry your work between devices it uses two things that already do the job well, a folder your cloud provider mirrors, and git. Both are optional.

Sync your settings through a folder

  1. Open Help > Personalise QUILL (or Preferences) and find “Where should QUILL store your data?”. It is the same page the first-run wizard shows.
  2. Choose “Choose a folder:”.
  3. Pick a folder that OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive or iCloud already keeps in step across your devices, or a folder on a USB drive you carry between computers.

QUILL writes its settings, snippets, dictionaries and keymap there, and your cloud provider or drive carries them to your other computers like everything else in that folder. This is the Data Location setting; there is nothing new to learn.

One important limit: QUILL cannot merge changes made on two devices at once. Don’t run QUILL on two machines pointed at the same synced folder at the same time. Treat it like any shared file, one writer at a time.

Sync a folder with GitHub

Tools > Git and GitHub > GitHub > Sync Folder with GitHub… works on any folder, such as a writing project or a research folder, not just a vault. Point it at a folder:

  • If the folder is already a git repository with a remote set up, QUILL commits your changes, pulls anyone else’s and pushes, all in the background, and tells you when it’s done.
  • If it isn’t set up yet, QUILL says so plainly and asks first, for example: “This folder is not a git repository yet. QUILL can set it up: this runs ‘git init’ in the folder, then adds the remote repository you provide as ‘origin’. Continue?” Say yes, paste your repository’s address (for example https://github.com/you/your-repo.git), and QUILL sets it up and syncs.
  • If the same file changed in both places, QUILL lists the conflicts and stops instead of guessing. Resolve them yourself (the conflict walker under Local Git helps), then run Sync Folder with GitHub again.

If you already use Sync Vault, this works exactly the same way, for any folder. Both use your own git installation and the credentials it already remembers (an SSH key, or a login your system’s git credential manager keeps). QUILL never asks for or stores a separate GitHub password or token for this. Disabled in Safe Mode.

Publishing

You can share what you write without leaving QUILL. This topic covers posting to Mastodon.

Posting to Mastodon

  1. Press the QUILL key (Ctrl+Shift+Grave) then Shift+P, or choose Tools > Share > Post to Mastodon…. QUILL takes your selection, or the whole document if nothing is selected, and opens a compose window.
  2. Edit the text if you like, pick the account to post from, and choose the visibility: Public, Unlisted, Followers only, or Direct. A live character count keeps track as you type.
  3. Press Post. Your post appears with “via QUILL” as its source.

The compose window also has a Post language picker beside the visibility choice. The default, “Default (instance)”, sends no language, so your server files the post under your account’s default language. Pick a language such as English or Italian to send its ISO 639-1 code, which keeps a post in one language from being filed under another.

The character count uses your account’s real limit on its own server, not the classic limit. QUILL asks the server once per session and remembers the answer, so a server that allows more (for example one with a 9999-character limit) shows the right count and does not block a longer post.

Adding a Mastodon account

The first time you post, QUILL offers to add an account. You can also open Tools > Share > Mastodon Accounts… at any time.

  1. Choose Add Account…, then enter your server (for example mastodon.social) and a friendly nickname. The nickname is what shows in the account picker.
  2. QUILL registers itself with your server and opens your browser. Sign in if needed, approve QUILL, and copy the authorization code your server shows.
  3. Paste that code back into QUILL. Your account is saved.

You can add several accounts, each with its own nickname, set a default, or remove one (which deletes its saved sign-in from this computer). Your sign-in is kept in the Windows Credential Manager, never in a plain file.

Proofread posts before sending. In Mastodon Accounts…, select an account and check Spell-check posts before sending. It is off by default and set per account, so you can turn it on for some accounts and not others. When it is on, pressing Post for that account first opens the Spelling Review (F7) on the post, and the post is sent only after you finish or skip the review.

Adding someone to a Mastodon list

Mastodon lists let you follow a group of accounts in a timeline of their own. To put someone on one of your lists:

  1. Choose Tools > Share > Add a User to a Mastodon List….
  2. Type their handle, such as @name@server, and press Enter. QUILL looks them up and fetches your lists.
  3. Choose the list from the list QUILL shows you, and press Enter.

QUILL says “Added”, the person and the list. Mastodon only lets you add someone you already follow, so if they are not on the list afterwards, follow them first (View Mastodon Profile, below, has a Follow button) and try again. If you have no lists yet, QUILL tells you; make one on your Mastodon server first.

Reading a Mastodon profile aloud

Open Tools > Share > View Mastodon Profile… and type a handle such as @name@server. QUILL shows the account’s name, whether each of you follows the other, a Follow or Unfollow button, the account’s Bio, and its Recent posts.

Everything there is tidied for listening. Mastodon sends bios and posts as web markup, which a screen reader would otherwise read aloud tags and all. QUILL turns them into plain text first, so you hear the words. In a link, you hear the part your server chose to show, not the long hidden tail.

Three more changes make the profile easier on the ear:

  • A pile of mentions is counted, not recited. A reply that starts by addressing several people reads as @alice and 2 more, then the message. You still learn who was addressed and how many, and you reach the first real word straight away. A reply that names one person is left as written.
  • Decorative characters are removed from names and posts. A screen reader says an emoji’s full name (“grinning face with smiling eyes”) every time it appears, in every row. QUILL strips emoji and similar decoration, and keeps accented letters, other alphabets, quotation marks, dashes and currency signs, which are part of real words. If a display name was nothing but decoration, QUILL uses the plain handle.
  • Each post is one line: when, then its first sentence. For example 3 minutes ago: Actually, that is wrong. The time is in plain words, so there is no timestamp to work out in your head, and the summary stops at the first sentence, so each arrow press gives you one post. A post with a content warning shows the warning instead of the text.

If the account is private, or your server does not share its posts, the profile still opens; the Recent posts list is simply not there.

Local Git

Tools > Git and GitHub > Local Git brings the two hardest parts of everyday git into QUILL as guided steps you can follow by ear: resolving a merge conflict, and reordering commits with an interactive rebase. None of it needs a GitHub account or the network; it works on any git repository on your computer.

Uncommitted changes

Uncommitted Changes… shows every file you have changed since your last commit, split into staged and unstaged. Select a file to read its changes in the same style as Compare Documents, instead of a raw diff. Press Stage or Unstage for the selected file, or Stage All to stage everything.

Resolving a merge conflict

Git marks a conflict with lines of <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>, which sound like line noise through a screen reader. Resolve Conflicts… walks you through every conflict in every affected file, one at a time: “Conflict 1 of 3: your version says X, their version says Y.” For each one you choose:

  • keep your version,
  • keep their version,
  • keep both, or
  • type your own replacement.

Move to the next or previous conflict as you go. When you’re done, QUILL writes the resolved file and stages it for you.

The same walker opens on its own if an Interactive Rebase… or a Sync Folder with GitHub stops because of a conflict, so you finish in one place.

Interactive rebase

Interactive Rebase… does the job of git rebase -i, which normally drops you in a text editor to reorder and mark up commits by eye. QUILL shows a real list instead, one commit per row:

  1. For each commit, choose an action from the dropdown: pick, squash, reword, or drop.
  2. Use Move Up and Move Down to change the order.
  3. Press Start Rebase when the plan is right.

If a step conflicts, the conflict walker opens; resolve it and the rebase carries on by itself. Abort Rebase puts your branch back exactly where it started if you change your mind partway.

More Local Git commands

  • Switch Branch… lists your local branches and switches to the one you choose. If you have uncommitted changes, QUILL warns you and offers to switch anyway and bring them along. It never quietly throws them away, and it doesn’t just refuse.
  • Stash Changes… / Manage Stashes… put your uncommitted work aside under a name you’ll recognize, then list, apply or drop any stash later, with no stash@{2} references to remember.
  • Who Wrote This Line… runs git blame on the line your cursor is on and tells you who last changed it, when, and the commit’s summary.
  • Start Bisect… / End Bisect runs a git bisect session as plain questions and answers. QUILL checks out a commit and asks “Is this version good or bad?” Answer, and it narrows the search until it tells you exactly which commit brought in the problem.

None of these commands has a default key, because every letter after the QUILL key is already taken. All twelve are in the command palette and on the Tools > Git and GitHub > Local Git menu, and you can give any of them your own key in the Keymap Editor.

Worktrees

A git repository is normally one folder holding one branch at a time. Switching branches rewrites every file in that folder to match the new branch, keeping the same names and paths.

A worktree is a second folder attached to the same repository, with a different branch checked out in it. The folders share one history, one set of branches and one set of stashes, but each has its own copy of the files. You might have quill on main and quill-feature-x on feature/x, side by side.

This matters more when you use a screen reader. Switch branches in place and the document you have open in QUILL is replaced by a different document with the same name. Someone looking at the screen sees the text change. With a screen reader nothing tells you: the paragraph under your review cursor now comes from another branch, in a file that still has the name of the one you opened. With a worktree, nothing under your cursor changes. Moving to other work means opening a different file, which you do and hear, instead of a file quietly becoming a different file.

Seeing what you have

Tools > Git and GitHub > Local Git > Worktrees… opens the list. QUILL says how many worktrees the repository has as the dialog opens, and each row reads as a whole sentence, so there are no columns to arrow across:

  • “Main worktree at S:\code\quill, on branch main”
  • “Linked worktree at S:\code\quill-feature-x, on branch feature/x”
  • “Linked worktree at D:\usb\quill-spike, on branch spike, locked: on a USB drive”
  • “Linked worktree at S:\code\quill-old, on branch old, missing from disk, ready to prune”

A worktree that is not on a branch reads as “not on a branch, at commit 3f9a21c”. After any action, QUILL speaks the result, rereads the list and puts focus back on it, so you never have to hunt for your place.

Creating one

Press New Worktree… in the list, or run Local Git: New Worktree… from the command palette to skip the list. The form asks for:

  • Folder for the new worktree: where the new folder should go. Type or paste it, or press Browse…. The field accepts whatever you paste: a path copied from File Explorer with the quotes still on, an %APPDATA%-style path, a file:// link, or a leading ~.
  • Branch to check out: a list of your local branches. Branches already checked out in another worktree are left out, because git won’t allow the same branch twice.
  • Create a new branch instead: check this to make a brand-new branch here instead of checking out an existing one.
  • New branch name and Start the new branch from: used only when the checkbox is checked. Leave the starting point blank to branch from where you are now, or name a branch, tag or commit to start from.

QUILL checks everything before it runs git, and tells you what is wrong if something is: a folder that already has files in it, a folder inside the repository itself (git won’t allow that), no branch chosen, or no new branch name typed.

Opening one

Select a worktree and press Open in QUILL, or just press Enter on the row. QUILL opens documents, not folders, so this means “open the same file from over there”. QUILL works out where your current document sits in its own worktree and opens the matching file in the one you chose. If that file doesn’t exist there (it is new on your branch, or nothing was open), QUILL says so and gives you a file picker already in the worktree’s folder.

Removing, locking and tidying up
  • Remove… deletes a worktree’s folder from your disk. The branch stays in the repository; you are removing the folder, not the work. QUILL always confirms first, with No as the default button, so pressing Enter out of habit never destroys anything.
  • If the worktree still has uncommitted changes, git refuses, and QUILL tells you so in plain language instead of forcing it. Only then does it ask a second, separate question: discard those changes and remove it anyway? That is two confirmations, never one.
  • Lock marks a worktree as “leave this alone”, with an optional reason you’ll hear later in the list. Do this for a worktree on a USB drive or a network share, which git would otherwise treat as a folder that vanished. The button reads Unlock when the selected worktree is already locked.
  • Prune forgets any worktree whose folder is really gone from disk and tells you which ones it tidied up. When there is nothing to do, it says “Nothing to tidy up: every worktree is still on disk.”
  • The main worktree (the repository folder itself) can never be removed or locked here; those buttons are unavailable while it is selected.
Good to know about worktrees
  • A branch can only be checked out in one worktree at a time. That is git’s rule. If you pick a branch that is open somewhere else, QUILL tells you which folder has it so you can open that folder instead.
  • A worktree cannot live inside the repository it belongs to. Put it beside the repository folder.
  • Removing a worktree with uncommitted changes is refused unless you confirm twice, as above.
  • Worktrees need git, like everything under Tools > Git and GitHub > Local Git, and they are disabled in Safe Mode.
Worktree keys

Neither worktree command has a default key, for the same reason as the other Local Git commands. Both are on Tools > Git and GitHub > Local Git and in the command palette (Local Git: Worktrees… and Local Git: New Worktree…), and you can give either a key in the Keymap Editor.

In the Worktrees dialog:

  • Tab and Shift+Tab move between the list and the buttons.
  • Up and Down arrow move through the worktrees.
  • Enter or Space on a row is the same as Open in QUILL.
  • Access keys: Alt+N New Worktree, Alt+O Open in QUILL, Alt+R Remove, Alt+L Lock or Unlock, Alt+P Prune.
  • Escape closes the dialog.

In New Worktree:

  • Alt+F the folder field, Alt+B Browse, Alt+C the branch chooser.
  • Alt+N the “create a new branch” checkbox, Alt+A the new branch name, Alt+R the starting point.
  • Enter creates the worktree, and Escape cancels.

Downloading git and the GitHub CLI

The Local Git commands, and the Codespaces and Copilot commands under Tools > Git and GitHub > GitHub, need git and gh (the GitHub CLI) on your computer. QUILL looks for copies you already have first: if git or gh is already on your system PATH, QUILL uses it and you need nothing more.

If you don’t have them, Help > Download Optional Components has a row for each:

  • Git: Windows only, a portable copy of Git for Windows, about 40 MB.
  • GitHub CLI: Windows and macOS, about 14 MB.

Both are exact copies of the official releases, checksum-verified like every other optional component. Download either one and its commands work straight away, with no separate install, no PATH changes and no restart. You can remove either one later from the same dialog; removing one never affects the other, even though they are stored in the same place.

Quill Radio and the QuillVille family

Internet radio is not part of QUILL. It is Quill Radio, a free app of its own in the QuillVille family, with its own window, its own keyboard-first design, and its own complete User Guide (open it from the app’s Help menu). The other companions are the same: Quill Weather, QUILL Audio Studio, Quill Inkwell, and the rest.

They share QUILL’s code, settings and data where that helps you. A station you favorite in Quill Radio, or an abbreviation you add in Quill Inkwell, is the same on both sides. Each app is documented in its own guide, not here.

The QuillVille menu sits just before Help in QUILL’s menu bar, and in every QuillVille app. It is where they all meet: it lists every app in the family, launches the ones you have, and offers to download the ones you don’t. That menu, and this short note, are all QUILL’s guide has to say about them.

QUILLBert found something: he opened the QuillVille menu looking for the way back to his document, and launched a radio station instead. He stayed for three songs. If that happens to you, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R tucks Quill Radio into the tray and the music keeps playing.

What you learned, and where to go next

You can now catch a thought in a sticky note from anywhere, find it again in the Sticky Notes Browser, and set up global hotkeys, including Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Q to show or hide QUILL. You know how to gather files in a notebook, organize a book in Story Studio, link your notes in a vault, move between formats, build tables in Table Studio, sync with a folder or GitHub, post to Mastodon, and handle conflicts, rebases and worktrees in Local Git.

To practise, open Help > Tutorials… (Ctrl+Alt+F1) and try “QUILL and the apps around it”. On the website, read Start an Accessible Vault, GitHub inside QUILL, Internet Radio with Quill Radio and Podcasts with QUILL Cast.

Next, Chapter 15, Help, updates and support, shows where to turn when you are stuck and how to keep QUILL up to date.

Chapter 15: Help, updates and support

This last chapter is about the help that is always within reach. You will meet the Help menu, the F1 key that explains whatever you are standing on, the guided tutorials, and the support form that puts you in touch with a real person. It also covers keeping QUILL up to date. Read it early if you like to know where the safety rails are, or come back to it the first time you feel stuck.

The Help menu

The Help menu is where QUILL turns into a guide. It is not a dead end with an About box at the bottom: most of what is on it does real work. The welcome guide teaches the basics, the keyboard reference shows the keys you actually have, the user guide gives you the full map, diagnostics capture what QUILL is doing right now, and Get Help from Support… turns all of that into a message somebody can answer.

The menu stays steady while you arrow through it quickly. QUILL waits until the menu closes before it updates anything on it.

Guides and references

  • Help on This Control (F1) tells you about whatever you are on. Chapter 2 has the details.
  • Announce Mode Shortcuts (press the QUILL key, then Shift+H) says the handful of keys that matter where you are right now: the browse-mode keys while you are in QUILL browse mode, the status bar keys while you are on the status bar, and the everyday editing keys otherwise.
  • Show Spoken Echo (Alt+Shift+E) shows the last things QUILL said, so you can read them at your own pace. Chapter 11 has more.
  • Open User Guide (Ctrl+Shift+F1) opens this guide as a document inside QUILL.
  • Open Welcome Guide opens a lighter getting-started document that knows which feature profile you are using.
  • Open Keyboard Reference builds a fresh list of shortcuts from the keys that are bound right now, so it always matches your setup.
  • Tutorials… (Ctrl+Alt+F1) opens the guided lessons. They have their own topic, Tutorials, later in this chapter.
  • What Can I Do Here? gives help that fits what you are doing at the moment.
  • Why Don’t I See a Feature? explains why a command is hidden by your feature profile.

Activity and Repeat Last Result (Shift+F9 and F9)

Activity… (Shift+F9) lists everything QUILL told you in this session, newest first. Each row says what you can do about it, with these buttons: Retry, Open Folder, Copy Details and Clear List.

  • If a settings file could not be saved, QUILL says so once, with the reason. Its row has a Retry that saves again and an Open Folder that shows you the folder on disk. When a later save works, QUILL tells you that too.
  • Background work that finishes after you closed its window lands here as a row to review, so the result is not lost.
  • Nothing in the list leaves this computer, and no document text is ever in it.

Repeat Last Result (F9) says the newest result that mattered again. That is the last thing QUILL itself told you, not the last thing your screen reader read. It also names what Activity offers for that result. The same two keys do the same thing in QUILL Lite, Quill Radio and QUILL Cast.

QUILLBee’s tip: Missed what QUILL just said because your screen reader talked over it? Press F9 and you will hear it again.

Status, diagnostics and setup

  • Status Page opens a live view of what QUILL is doing right now. The Application Status page topic in this guide describes it.
  • Save Diagnostics… writes a diagnostics bundle on this computer. You can look through it before you share it with anyone.
  • Feature Profiles gathers the profile commands:
    • Switch Profile… (Alt+Shift+P) chooses another profile.
    • Profile Health Check… gives a short report on your profile: which one is active, and whether any command has been left without a feature to belong to, or switched off when it should not be. Most of the time it ends with “No coverage problems found”. It is mainly useful when support asks you to read it to them.
    • Manage Individual Features… (Ctrl+Alt+F10) turns single features on and off.
    • Undo Last Profile Change puts back the profile you had before your last change. If there is nothing to undo, it says so.
    • Reset to Essential Profile goes back to the smallest, simplest profile. It asks first, with No already chosen.
  • Personalise QUILL… is the first-run setup wizard. Run it again whenever you like to adjust your keyboard pack, feature profile, remote access, AI, reading and accessibility, writing tools, data location, and startup behaviour. Personalising QUILL walks through it.
  • Get Help from Support… (Ctrl+Alt+F2) opens the support form. When you have filled it in, QUILL hands the message to your own mail program, addressed to support@community-access.org. A person reads and answers it. It is not a public issue tracker, and you do not need an account anywhere. The steps are in Get Help from Support, step by step.

Updates, About and notices

  • Check for Updates… checks the signed update list, offers you the download, and can close QUILL so setup runs straight away. Installed and portable copies are handled differently; Checking for Updates explains both.
  • About Quill shows the version, publisher details, and the third-party components QUILL uses, each with its license and version. The version has a build number, such as 1.0.0 (build 2): the build number tells you which build of a version you have, and a fix shipped without a new version number comes as a newer build that Check for Updates offers you.
  • Open Third-Party Notices opens the full notices document, with tables of those components and the text of every bundled license.

On a Mac

On macOS the Help menu is the system Help menu, so the usual Cmd+? shortcut opens it. (See Appendix D, Notes from earlier versions.)

Help, Learning, and Daily Confidence

Nobody remembers everything, and QUILL does not expect you to. There are several layers of help, and you can reach each one from the keyboard.

  • F1 gives help on the control that has focus. It works anywhere in QUILL.
  • Open User Guide (Ctrl+Shift+F1) is for when you want the full map.
  • Open Welcome Guide is for when you want a lighter introduction.
  • Open Keyboard Reference is for when you want the exact keys you have now.
  • Key Cheatsheet (Ctrl+F1) gives you a quick list of shortcuts.
  • What Can I Do Here? (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F1) gives help on the spot, for the document you are in.
  • Why Don’t I See a Feature? is for when a command seems to have disappeared.
  • Why Is This Unavailable? (Alt+F1) is for something you can see but cannot use. Move to the greyed-out button or menu item and press Alt+F1, and QUILL tells you why it is turned off.

That last one is worth remembering. When something you expected is missing, it tells you why, usually because your feature profile hides it, so you are not left guessing.

Context-Sensitive Help (F1)

Press F1 on any control in QUILL that can take focus, and a small help window opens. It tells you:

  1. The dialog you are in, when you are inside one: its name and a plain summary of what it does, so you always know where you are.
  2. The focused control: what it is, how it works, and which keys apply to it.

All of that text is in one read-only field, so your screen reader reads the whole thing in one go when the window opens. There are no headings to move past.

From the help window:

  • Press Escape, or Enter on Close, to go back to where you were.
  • Tab to Open User Guide and press it to jump to the part of this guide that covers the control.

Here is how the Help keys fit together:

Key What it does
F1 Help on the control that has focus
Ctrl+Shift+F1 Open the full User Guide
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F1 Open What Can I Do Here? for the document you are in
Ctrl+F1 Open the Key Cheatsheet
Shift+F1 Open About Quill

A few things worth knowing:

  • In the main editor, F1 tells you the editor shortcuts and some writing tips.
  • In dialogs such as Preferences, Find/Replace and Spell Check, F1 names both the dialog and the setting you are on.
  • In the Personalise QUILL wizard, F1 on any control explains what that setting does and what you can change later.
  • When you use a menu and come back to the editor, QUILL remembers which control had focus, so F1 still talks about the right one.

Personalising QUILL

The Personalise QUILL wizard runs on its own the first time QUILL starts. You can run it again at any time from Help > Personalise QUILL….

It has six short pages, or five if you leave AI writing help off on the Extras page:

  1. Welcome introduces what the wizard covers.
  2. Intent is the page that matters most. It asks one question: What kind of writing do you do? and shows a list of seven starting points. Arrow up and down the list. As you move, a large read-only text area below it changes to tell you, in plain English, exactly what you will get if you choose that one. No feature codes, no jargon, and no list of what you will miss out on. Just what you get.
  3. Extras offers a few optional extras, such as AI writing help, Braille Mode and typing automation. You only see the ones your starting point does not already include. Each is a single checkbox, and checking one adds a sentence to the preview, so you always know what you are agreeing to.
  4. AI Provider appears only if you turned AI on in Extras. It asks for your provider and your API key. The providers are Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Google Gemini, OpenRouter (many models), and Ollama, which runs models on your own computer or connects to an Ollama-compatible cloud host. Your key is kept safely in the Windows Credential Manager, not in a settings file. You can skip this page and add a key later.
  5. Keyboard and Sound is where you choose a keyboard pack and whether QUILL plays sound cues. QUILL detects your screen reader and picks accessible defaults for you.
  6. Summary lets you check every choice before anything happens. It is plain text: your profile name, which features are on, which Quillins are turned on, your keyboard pack and your sound setting. Use Back to change any page. Nothing in QUILL changes until you press Finish.

Every page starts with a heading that takes focus, so you land on the page title first. The preview is a read-only document, so VoiceOver on the Mac does not call it an editable text field.

Important: nothing is saved until you press Finish. If you close or cancel the wizard, none of your settings change.

Profiles explained

QUILL comes with eleven built-in feature profiles: the ten described under Choosing a profile, plus the QUILL Lite profile. Each one starts you at a different amount of features and a different level of accessibility support. The wizard offers seven plain-English starting points that lead to them; its Writer starting point is the Casual Writer profile. You can switch profile at any time from Tools > Customize and Support > Profiles and Features… or by pressing Alt+Shift+P.

Choosing a profile, earlier in this guide, says who each one is for.

Tutorials

Help > Tutorials… (Ctrl+Alt+F1) opens 29 guided tutorials: 159 steps, about 147 minutes in all. They cover the parts of QUILL worth learning first, in the order you would naturally learn them. They are not a second copy of this guide. A guide can tell you what something does. It cannot tell you what to do next, because it cannot see what you have already done. The Tutorials window can.

How the lessons work

  • They show the keys you have. A step names the command it is about, and the key is filled in when the step is shown. If you have rebound a key, the tutorial says your key.
  • Try it runs the step. Any step that names a command can be carried out from the lesson. A tutorial can open a window for you and then talk you through what you are looking at.
  • Follow me notices when you have done it. Check Follow me and the lesson keeps an eye on QUILL, once a second. It watches what changed, never which key you pressed, so however you do the step, it says what it saw (“Done: the document changed”) and reads you the next one. It never takes over the keyboard, and nothing is marked. Every step still has Next, so if the check never notices, it costs you one keypress.

The Tutorials window is an ordinary window, not a wizard. Leave it open, go to your document, do the step there, and hear the lesson move on in the background.

Finding a lesson

The lessons are in six tracks, in teaching order. Each row says how many steps it has, about how long it takes, and whether you have finished it. The filter box narrows the list: every word you type has to appear somewhere in a tutorial. Type here to see only the tutorials about the window you came from.

Your place is kept

Close a lesson half way through and it opens at the same step next time. Finishing a lesson is remembered separately from where you are in it. Forget my progress clears all of that and changes nothing else. Nothing about your progress leaves this computer.

Reading instead of doing

Read it all shows a whole tutorial as one page of text. The whole book as a document opens all 24 as one page. It is made from the same lessons the window teaches, so the two always agree. It also comes as tutorials.md beside this guide. The document gives the keys QUILL comes with; only the window knows the ones you have rebound.

Quill Radio, QUILL Cast and Quill Weather each have their own lessons, opened with the same Ctrl+Alt+F1 in every app. QUILL’s own set covers your first hour, writing, reading, how much QUILL says, the assistant, and the things you meet in your second week. The menus and the command palette cover the rest.

QUILL, Step by Step

Prefer to learn by listening? QUILL, Step by Step is a separate, slower manual written to be read aloud. It has seventeen short chapters, one skill each, with practice moments and recaps, and none of this guide’s reference tables. It comes beside this guide as Markdown, HTML and EPUB. The EPUB opens straight into ElevenReader, Voice Dream or any reading app, so it can talk you through QUILL while your hands stay on the keyboard.

Get Help from Support, step by step

Use this whenever QUILL does something you did not expect, when you are stuck, when you have a question, or when you want to suggest something. It is the same form QUILL Lite and Quill Radio use, and it reaches a person at Community Access, not a public issue tracker.

  1. Choose Help > Get Help from Support…, or press Ctrl+Alt+F2 from anywhere in QUILL. On the Help menu its letter is L, because G already opens the user guide. If you gave it a different key in the past, that key still works.
  2. The form opens on What kind of message. Choose one of: something is broken, a question, an accessibility problem, or an idea or request. This only helps the message reach the right person.
  3. Tab to Subject and type one short line, as you would for an email.
  4. Tab to What happened and describe it in your own words. This is the part a person reads first.
  5. What you expected and Steps to reproduce are optional. If you can give steps, they help more than anything else.
  6. Your email address is optional too. The message goes from your own mail account, so support can already reply to you there. Only fill this in if you want the reply to go somewhere else.
  7. Screen reader is filled in from whatever is running. Change it if it is wrong.
  8. Below the fields, QUILL tells you what else is included: its version, your Windows version and, when this computer is connected to QUILL’s free AI, your QUILL AI support ID. That is the number support asks for first.
  9. Press Send (or Enter). Your own mail program opens with the whole message written and addressed to support@community-access.org. Nothing is sent until you press Send in your mail program. Read it over, attach a diagnostics bundle if you like, or close it if you change your mind. Pressing Escape in the form cancels without writing anything.

If something gets in the way

  • If a required field is empty, QUILL tells you which one and leaves you in the form.
  • If the message is too long for a mail link, your mail program opens with the start of it. QUILL puts the complete text on your clipboard and tells you to paste it in with Control V.
  • If this computer has no mail program set up (you only use webmail, say), QUILL shows you the address and puts the whole message on your clipboard, so nothing you typed is lost.
  • Writing to support@community-access.org yourself always works just as well.

Want to share more detail? Help > Save Diagnostics… writes a bundle with private details removed, which you review and can attach to the email.

No more GitHub reports

QUILL no longer files GitHub issues for you, and no copy of QUILL carries a built-in GitHub “reporting token”. Your own GitHub sign-in, for QUILL’s GitHub features, is separate and has not changed. Check for Updates used to offer to “restore the token” by reinstalling the same version; that offer has gone too, and Check for Updates now only ever offers a newer version.

Checking for Updates

QUILL can check for updates and install them while you carry on working.

Manual update check

To check for updates now:

  1. Press Alt+H to open the Help menu.
  2. Press U for Check for Updates.
  3. If a newer version is out, QUILL tells you and asks whether to download it.
  4. If you say yes, QUILL downloads it in the background and tells you when it is ready.
  5. The next time you close and reopen QUILL, the update is applied for you.

Automatic update checks

QUILL can check for updates each time it starts:

  1. Press Alt+E to open the Edit menu.
  2. Press Shift+S for Settings.
  3. In the Updates section, turn on Check for updates on startup.

With automatic checks on, QUILL lets you know quietly when a new version is available, and you download it when it suits you.

Update size and speed

QUILL uses small incremental updates (“micro-updates”) instead of a full reinstall. They often download in seconds, and your settings, documents and preferences are kept.

Updating a portable copy

If you run the portable copy of QUILL, Check for Updates notices and offers the portable .zip for the new version instead of the installer. It downloads to your updates folder, and QUILL offers an Extract now button that unzips it into a ready-to-run folder next to your current one.

Putting a portable update in place is always a job you do yourself. QUILL never replaces its own files while it is running, because they may be locked while it is open. After extracting, copy your data folder into the new version’s folder and start QUILL from there.

Installed copies keep getting the installer, which does put itself in place when you run it.

Staying on a release channel

By default, QUILL follows the Stable channel and only offers you finished versions. To try new features early, see Release Channels below.

Release Channels

QUILL comes in three flavours, and you choose which one this copy follows. They’re called release channels.

  • Stable is the version we recommend. It has been checked with JAWS and NVDA, and it’s what most people use. Every copy starts here.
  • Beta gets new features a few weeks early. It’s mostly finished, but some things may not work right yet.
  • Dev is the work in progress, sometimes several builds a week. Things will break. Only choose it if a developer asked you to, or you enjoy testing.

Choosing a channel

  1. Open the Help menu, then choose Release Channel… (press Alt+H, then I). You can also get there from Settings: on the Administration page, the Release channel row has a Change release channel… button.
  2. Arrow through Stable, Beta and Dev. As you move, the box below tells you what each one means and what choosing it would do. Nothing changes yet.
  3. Press Switch to move. Press Close, or Escape, to leave everything as it was.

If you choose Beta or Dev, QUILL shows a short warning first: what could go wrong, how your settings are protected, and how to come back. Read it, check the I understand box, then choose Move to Beta (or Move to Dev). Stay on Stable changes nothing, and so does Escape.

Beta and Dev versions aren’t signed, so when you install one, Windows SmartScreen may warn that it comes from an unknown publisher; that’s expected, and choosing More info, then Run anyway, installs it.

What happens when you move to Beta or Dev

  • QUILL saves a copy of your settings, keys and preferences first. If it can’t, it stays where it is and tells you why. Your documents aren’t copied, and updates don’t change them.
  • QUILL then checks for updates on the new channel straight away, and offers you the newest Beta or Dev version if there is one. Nothing is installed unless you say so.
  • From then on, Check for Updates offers you versions from your channel. On Stable, you’re never offered a test version.

If you installed a Beta version yourself, QUILL notices the first time it checks for updates. It puts itself on the Beta channel and tells you so, and you can change it in the Release Channel window whenever you like.

Updates on Beta and Dev

When QUILL’s startup check finds a new version, it downloads it for you, as it always has, so it is ready when you are. It never installs anything without asking: when the download is done, it says so and shows you what’s new, and you choose when to install.

On Beta and Dev, it waits instead of downloading on a metered connection, during Quiet Hours, and while Quill Radio is recording. The notifications list and Update History tell you why it waited.

If an update doesn’t start

After an update, QUILL checks that the new version really opens. If it doesn’t open within two minutes, the update undoes itself and puts back the version you had. The next time QUILL starts, it tells you so. Nothing of yours is changed, and Update History has the details.

To make this possible, QUILL keeps a copy of the installer for the version you have: on Beta and Dev for as long as you have that version, and on Stable for a week or three starts after each update. That copy takes about 200 MB of disk space, which Stable gives back once the week or the three starts are up. After an update, the previous installer is kept until the new version has started three times, or for a week, and then it is deleted.

Coming back to Stable

Open Release Channel again and choose Stable.

  • If the version you have is already a Stable one, you’re back straight away, and nothing is installed.
  • If you have a newer Beta or Dev version, QUILL checks whether Stable can read everything you have saved. If it can, choose Go back to (the Stable version) now, and QUILL downloads Stable and offers to install it. Your settings and keys come with you.
  • If Stable can’t read something yet, QUILL says so and gives you two safe choices. Wait for Stable keeps the version you have, stops test versions, and moves you to Stable by itself as soon as Stable catches up. It tells you when that happens. Use the copy from (the day you joined) puts back the copy of your settings and keys saved when you joined, then installs Stable. Anything you changed since then won’t be in it, but a copy of how things are right now is saved first, so nothing is thrown away.
  • If there’s no saved copy, waiting is the only choice, and the window says so.

Moving your other apps together

If QUILL Lite, Quill Radio or QUILL Cast is on this computer too, the Release Channel window lists it under Also move my other QuillVille apps on this computer. Check any you’d like to move in the same step. Every box starts unchecked.

Those apps run on one shared engine. When one of them moves to Beta or Dev, it gets its own copy of that engine, so the apps you leave on Stable are never touched. That copy takes about 335 MB of disk space, and it goes away by itself when the last of them comes back to Stable. QUILL itself doesn’t use the shared engine, so moving QUILL on its own needs no extra space.

Update History

The Update History button in the Release Channel window shows what the updater has done for QUILL: channel changes, the copies of your settings it saved, and so on. It’s a record to read; nothing in it changes anything.

Your privacy

Switching channels sends nothing about you. When QUILL checks for updates, the only thing it sends is a request for the list of versions.

Beta Feedback and Bug Reporting

QUILL is ready for serious beta use, and it has a real support starting point built in.

What you can use today

  • Recovery state.
  • Notifications.
  • Extraction review.
  • Exporting a bad-extraction package, for problems with extraction.
  • Save Diagnostics…, a general command that writes a bundle on this computer.
  • Get Help from Support… (Ctrl+Alt+F2), which writes a message to support@community-access.org in your own mail program, with details about your setup already filled in. It used to be called Report a Bug….
  • A diagnostics runbook and a documented support process.

QUILL helps you gather diagnostics on your own computer, check what you are about to share, and start a clear support message without leaving QUILL.

What is still to come

QUILL does not yet have a secure way to upload straight from the app without signing in anywhere. For now, the Help > Get Help from Support… form is the one route: it emails support through your own mail program and never files anything on GitHub. A fuller route that needs no GitHub sign-in is planned:

  1. a Community Access feedback form on a secure (HTTPS) web page,
  2. an optional upload of a diagnostics bundle you have reviewed,
  3. a plain-language bug template with a summary of your setup and the steps to reproduce the problem,
  4. alongside the in-app Help > Get Help from Support… form.

Control Reference

The Control Reference lists every control in QUILL that can take focus, grouped by section. For each one it says what the control does, which keys apply to it, and which part of this guide covers it in depth.

The full list is in the Control Reference.

If you build QUILL yourself, you can regenerate it after adding new help topics:

python -m quill.tools.build_docs

What you learned, and where to go next

You now know your way around the Help menu, including Activity (Shift+F9) and Repeat Last Result (F9). F1 explains any control, What Can I Do Here? helps on the spot, and the Personalise QUILL wizard can be run again whenever your needs change. You can send a message to a real person with Get Help from Support (Ctrl+Alt+F2), and you know how to check for updates.

To practise, open Help > Tutorials… (Ctrl+Alt+F1) and try “Getting unstuck” and “Do anything by name” from the Your first hour track. On the website, Your first hour with QUILL covers the same ground at a gentler pace.

That is the last chapter. The appendices follow, including the Glossary of QUILL Terms and Getting help, for whenever you need them.

A last word

The best way to get to know QUILL is to use it on something real: a note you care about, a PDF you scanned and need to check, an EPUB chapter you want to find your way around, a Markdown file that needs tidying, or a web page you want to make easier to use.

I would like QUILL to feel like a good guide sitting beside you while you work, never one standing in your way. If it does its job, you will spend less time wondering what it can do and more time on what you want to write next.

Acknowledgments

QUILL stands on the shoulders of the screen-reader-first editors that came before it. The keyboard-first way of comparing documents, and selecting with F8 from an anchor, were inspired by EdSharp and Boxer. I am grateful to those projects and the people who made them, for showing what an accessible, keyboard-driven editor can be.

Appendix A: The QUILL Developer Console

This appendix is for people who like to script and automate. Nobody needs it to write, and if you never open the console you are missing nothing you use every day. If you are a developer, a power user, an accessibility tester or someone building a Quillin, read on. The QUILL Developer Console (QDC for short) lets you look inside the running editor and drive it from code.

What the QDC is

The Developer Console is a scripting window built into QUILL. You can inspect and automate the editor while it runs, without rebuilding anything or adding temporary menu items.

It is switched off by default for the Essential, Casual Writer and Reader and Student profiles. You will find it under the Developer, Power Text and Full QUILL profiles.

There are two consoles:

  • Python console. Runs inside QUILL, with full access to the scripting API through the name q. Its prompt is >>>, and ... while you are in the middle of a block.
  • TypeScript console. Runs through a Node subprocess. Its API is asynchronous and is called quill. Its prompt is ts>, and ts*> while an async operation is still running.

Both share the same transcript window, and both speak through QUILL’s usual announcements.

Opening the console

Choose Tools > Advanced > Developer Console > Open Python Console or Tools > Advanced > Developer Console > Open TypeScript Console.

From the Command Palette, the commands are quill.console.openPython and quill.console.openTypeScript.

The console opens as its own dialog. Press Esc to send focus back to the editor. The dialog stays open, and keeps everything you defined, until you close it yourself.

Console layout

Press F6 to move between the five areas of the console:

  1. Transcript. Read-only. Shows prompts, output, errors and return values.
  2. Input. One line by default. Shift+Enter adds a new line, so you can type a block of several lines.
  3. Language selector. Switches between Python and TypeScript.
  4. Status line. The current language, prompt state, active document and worker status.
  5. Buttons. Run, Clear, Copy transcript, Save transcript, Insert snippet, Help and Close.

Keyboard reference

These keys work inside the console window.

Key Action
Enter Execute current command
Shift+Enter Insert newline (multi-line input)
Ctrl+Enter Force execute multi-line block
Up / Down Previous / next history (when cursor is at line boundary)
Ctrl+L Clear transcript
Ctrl+Shift+C Copy transcript
Ctrl+S Save transcript
Ctrl+F Find in transcript
F6 Move between transcript, input, status, and buttons
Esc Return focus to editor
F1 Console help
Ctrl+Space Trigger completion

Python console

Available names

These names are ready for you as soon as the console opens:

Name What it is
q Primary QUILL scripting API, start here
app Application-level read-mostly object
commands Command registry facade
doc Active document snapshot
editor Active editor snapshot
sel Current selection snapshot
caret Current caret snapshot
profile Active feature profile snapshot
settings Safe settings facade
diagnostics Diagnostics facade
a11y Announcement / testing facade
log Console-safe logger
wx wx module (Developer profile only)

doc, sel and caret are read-only snapshots, taken at the moment they were captured. They refresh when the active document changes. Otherwise, call q.refresh_context() to pull in the current state.

The q API also has these facades: q.selection, q.doc, q.editor, q.settings, q.profile, q.bookmarks, q.quillins, q.macros (with q.begin_macro and q.end_macro), q.spell, q.diagnostics, q.a11y, q.commands, q.focus and q.support, plus q.describe_command.

Basic operations

Insert text at the cursor:

>>> q.insert_text("Hello from QUILL.")

Replace the current selection:

>>> q.replace_selection("Replacement text")

Jump to a line:

>>> q.goto_line(42)

Run a built-in command by its ID:

>>> q.run_command("quill.document.wordCount")

Send a screen-reader announcement:

>>> q.a11y.announce("Test announcement.")

Inspecting state

Read the name of the active document:

>>> doc.name
'notes.txt'

Read the current selection:

>>> sel.text
'selected words here'

Read where the caret is (line and column both start at 1):

>>> caret.line, caret.column
(12, 5)

Search for commands by keyword:

>>> commands.search("spell")
['quill.spell.check', 'quill.spell.addWord', 'quill.spell.nextError']

Get a diagnostic summary, which is handy when you are asking for support:

>>> q.support.diagnostic_summary()

Accessibility diagnostics

Hear again what QUILL last announced:

>>> q.a11y.last_announcements()
['Title Case applied', '5 words selected']

Describe where focus is right now:

>>> q.focus.describe()
'Editor: notes.txt, line 12, col 5, no selection'

Multi-line blocks

Press Shift+Enter to add new lines, then Enter or Ctrl+Enter to run the block:

>>> def count_words(text):
...     return len(text.split())
...
>>> count_words(doc.text)
487

When a command runs too long

If something you type into the Python console runs away, a loop that never ends say, QUILL stops it after Python console execution timeout seconds (Settings > Administration) and tells you “Stopped after 30 seconds.” It is 30 to begin with, and you can set anything from 5 to 300. A command that is waiting on the system, such as a long sleep, stops as soon as that wait is over.

Macro recording

You can record a run of commands as a macro and use it again later:

>>> q.begin_macro("Clean OCR text")
>>> q.run_command("quill.text.normalizeUnicode")
>>> q.run_command("quill.text.dehyphenateLines")
>>> q.run_command("quill.text.reflowParagraphs")
>>> q.end_macro()
Macro saved: "Clean OCR text"

TypeScript console

The TypeScript console needs Node.js on your PATH. If QUILL cannot find it, it tells you so and offers to help you install it.

TypeScript prompt behavior

ts> await quill.insertText("Hello.");
ts*>
Result: undefined

ts> means the console is ready. ts*> means an async operation is still in flight. Results and errors land in the transcript by themselves.

Available globals

Global What it is
quill Async QUILL scripting proxy
console Captured: .log(), .warn(), .error() appear in transcript
setTimeout / clearTimeout Standard timer
AbortController For cancellable operations

Basic TypeScript operations

Insert text:

ts> await quill.insertText("Hello from TypeScript.");

Replace the selection:

ts> await quill.replaceSelection("Replacement text");

Jump to a line:

ts> await quill.gotoLine(42);

Run a built-in command:

ts> await quill.runCommand("quill.markdown.normalizeHeadings");

Inspecting state from TypeScript

ts> const doc = await quill.activeDocument();
ts> console.log(doc.name);
notes.txt
ts> const stats = await quill.documentStats();
ts> console.log(`${stats.words} words, ${stats.lines} lines`);
487 words, 38 lines

Multi-line TypeScript

Press Shift+Enter to build a block over several lines, then Ctrl+Enter to run it:

ts> const text = await quill.getText();
ts> const words = text.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
ts> await quill.announce(`${words.length} words`);

TypeScript type definitions

QUILL comes with a file called quill-console.d.ts. If you have Node.js and a code editor that understands TypeScript, copy the file into your project and you get completion:

// quill is typed as:
interface QuillConsoleApi {
  insertText(text: string): Promise<void>;
  replaceSelection(text: string): Promise<void>;
  gotoLine(line: number): Promise<void>;
  runCommand(commandId: string, args?: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;
  activeDocument(): Promise<QuillDocumentSnapshot>;
  documentStats(): Promise<QuillDocumentStats>;
  announce(text: string): Promise<void>;
}

Screen-reader notes

  • New output in the transcript is announced, and focus stays where it is.
  • Errors are announced starting with the word “Error”.
  • Return values are announced starting with the word “Result”.
  • Long output is summed up in the announcement. Read the transcript with your screen reader for the full text.
  • Ctrl+Shift+C copies the transcript at any time.
  • The console speaks through Prism, the same announcement path every other part of QUILL uses.
  • Every control is a standard Windows control. Nothing is custom-drawn.

Console safety settings

Open them with Tools > Advanced > Developer Console > Console Safety Settings, or run the command quill.console.openSafetySettings.

Setting Default Notes
Python console enabled Profile-dependent Off for Essential / Casual Writer
TypeScript console enabled Profile-dependent Off except Developer profile
Require developer profile On Prevents accidental access in the Casual Writer profile
Max execution time (Python) 30 s Hard kill after timeout
Max execution time (TypeScript) 30 s Worker restart after timeout
Allow wx module access Developer profile only Not available in any other profile
Remote console Locked off Not available in QUILL 1.x

Transcript commands

You can run these from the Command Palette while the console is open.

Command What it does
quill.console.copyTranscript Copy entire transcript to clipboard
quill.console.saveTranscript Save transcript to a file
quill.console.clear Clear the transcript
quill.console.saveInputAsSnippet Save the current input as a named snippet
quill.console.insertSnippet Insert a saved snippet into input
quill.console.runSelection Run selected text in the transcript as a command
quill.console.runCurrentDocument Run the active QUILL document as a script
quill.console.showContext Print current snapshot values to transcript
quill.console.resetNamespace Reset the Python namespace (clears all variables)
quill.console.restartTypeScriptWorker Kill and restart the Node worker

For Quillin authors

The console is a good place to try out a Quillin while you build it. Load your Quillin, open the Python console, and look at its manifest and the commands it adds:

>>> from quill.core.quillins.loader import get_loader
>>> loader = get_loader()
>>> ext = loader.get_extension("com.example.myextension")
>>> ext.manifest
ExtensionManifest(id='com.example.myextension', runtime='python', ...)
>>> ext.manifest.contributes.commands
(ExtensionCommand(id='ext.myext.run', title='My Command', ...),)

Run one of its commands straight through the command registry:

>>> q.run_command("ext.myext.run")

Then check what it announced:

>>> q.a11y.last_announcements()
['My command completed: 3 items processed']

For a Node.js Quillin, the TypeScript console is the natural place to test:

ts> await quill.runCommand("ext.myext.nodeHandler");
ts> // Check the last announcement
ts> const ann = await quill.lastAnnouncement();
ts> console.log(ann);

What the console can and cannot do yet

The console is built and working under the Developer, Power Text and Full QUILL profiles, at Tools > Advanced > Developer Console. Here is what you get today:

  • The Python console and its console window.
  • The TypeScript console, running through a Node subprocess.
  • The q scripting API: the text, navigation and command methods, plus the facades q.selection, q.doc, q.editor, q.settings, q.profile, q.bookmarks, q.quillins, q.macros (with q.begin_macro and q.end_macro), q.spell, q.diagnostics, q.a11y, q.commands, q.focus and q.support, plus q.describe_command.

Some examples in this appendix were written for a fuller API than the console has today. If a call shown here does not work, the list above is the one to trust. The full scripting contract, with its own map of what is implemented, is in docs/quillins.md.

Where to go next

The thinking behind the console, and the plans for it, are in Appendix E, Developer Console design document. If you build Quillins, docs/quillins.md is your reference.

Appendix B: Writing skills for QUILL

This appendix shows you how to write, check and share your own skills. A skill lives in a .sqp file (Skill Quill Pack). It is a multi-step AI workflow, written in plain Markdown. If you can write a prompt, you can write a skill.

What a skill is

A QUILL prompt is one instruction. A skill is a short conversation: a series of instructions, where each step can see what the step before it produced.

A skill is the right tool when:

  • You want to analyse your text first, then act on what the analysis found.
  • You want to gather information in one step and write with it in the next.
  • You want to check something (is this a question or a statement?) and go a different way depending on the answer.
  • You want a better result on the same task, by giving the model context it built for itself in an earlier step.

Your first skill

Create a file called my-first-skill.sqp and open it in QUILL. Type this in:

---
schema: quill.skill/1
name: Explain Then Simplify
description: Explains the selected text in plain terms, then simplifies it further.
author: Your Name
version: 1.0.0
---

# Step 1: Explain

Explain the following text as if the reader has no prior knowledge. Use simple
vocabulary and short sentences. Aim for 50-80 words.

Text to explain:
{selection}

# Step 2: Simplify further

The explanation below is good, but we need it even simpler. Rewrite it so a
twelve-year-old would understand it immediately. Keep the core meaning.

Explanation to simplify:
{step1.output}

```output
format: text
label: Plain-language explanation
accept_into: clipboard

The part between the two `---` lines is the front matter: the skill's name and
details. Each line that starts with `# Step` begins a new step. `{selection}`
is your selected text, and `{step1.output}` is whatever step 1 produced.

Save the file, then check it with the validator:

```powershell
python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator my-first-skill.sqp

If all is well, you will see:

my-first-skill.sqp: OK

Adding parameters

Parameters let the person running the skill choose options first. Before step 1 begins, QUILL shows a small dialog that asks for those choices.

Here is the same skill with a choice of reading level added:

---
schema: quill.skill/1
name: Explain Then Simplify
description: Explains and simplifies selected text at a chosen reading level.
author: Your Name
version: 1.0.0
parameters:
  - name: level
    label: Target reading level
    type: choice
    choices: [Grade 4, Grade 6, Grade 8]
    default: Grade 6
---

# Step 1: Explain

Explain the following text so it is accessible at {parameters.level} reading level.
Use simple vocabulary and short sentences. Aim for 50-80 words.

Text to explain:
{selection}

# Step 2: Simplify further

Rewrite the explanation below to be even clearer. Target: {parameters.level}.
Keep the core meaning intact.

{step1.output}

```output
format: text
label: Plain-language explanation
accept_into: clipboard

Now `{parameters.level}` can be used in both steps. Its value is whatever the
user picked in the dialog.

There are five kinds of parameter:

| Type | UI control | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | Single-line text field | A keyword or name |
| `multiline` | Multi-line text area | A block of context |
| `choice` | Drop-down list | Reading level, tone, language |
| `bool` | Checkbox | Include citations: yes/no |
| `number` | Numeric field | Word count target |

### Using the input block

A long piece of text can bury the instruction it belongs to. The `input` block
adds the data after the instruction, so the step stays easy to read:

```markdown
# Step 1: Extract key claims

Read the following document and list the five most important claims it makes.
Number each claim. One sentence per claim.

```input
{document}

Without the `input` block you would write:

```markdown
# Step 1: Extract key claims

Read the following document and list the five most important claims it makes.
Number each claim. One sentence per claim.

Document:
{document}

Both do the same thing. The input block is just tidier when the data is long.

Branching on an answer

A condition block sends the skill down one path or another, depending on what a step produced.

# Step 1: Detect intent

Read the following text. Is it asking a question, or making a statement?
Answer with exactly one word: "question" or "statement".

```input
{selection}
if: "{step1.output}" contains "question"
then: step2
else: step3

Step 2: Answer the question

Answer this question clearly and concisely: {selection}

format: text
label: Answer
accept_into: clipboard

Step 3: Expand the statement

Expand the following statement into a full paragraph with supporting detail: {selection}

format: text
label: Expanded statement
accept_into: clipboard

Here is what happens. After step 1 runs, QUILL checks the condition. If the
output contains "question", it jumps to step 2. Otherwise it jumps to step 3.
Whichever step runs last is the one that produces the result.

You can use these operators in a condition:

| Operator | Matches when |
| --- | --- |
| `contains` | Subject contains value (case-insensitive) |
| `equals` | Subject exactly matches value (case-insensitive) |
| `starts_with` | Subject starts with value |
| `ends_with` | Subject ends with value |
| `length_gt` | Subject length > number |
| `length_lt` | Subject length < number |
| `is_empty` | Subject is blank |

### Controlling the output

The `output` block on the last step decides what happens to the result.

```markdown
```output
format: text
label: Rewritten paragraph
accept_into: selection

It has three settings:

- `format`: `text` (the default), `list` (the AI should return a bulleted or
  numbered list), or `json` (the AI should return valid JSON).
- `accept_into`: what happens when the user presses Accept in the result
  dialog. `selection` replaces the current selection in the editor.
  `clipboard` copies the result to the clipboard. `none` just shows it,
  read-only (this is the default).
- `label`: the heading of the result dialog, so the user knows what they are
  reviewing.

### A complete example, Accessible Rewrite

Here is the "Accessible Rewrite" skill that comes with QUILL, in full.

```markdown
---
schema: quill.skill/1
name: Accessible Rewrite
description: Rewrites selected text for plain-language accessibility.
author: QUILL Project
version: 1.0.0
parameters:
  - name: reading_level
    label: Target reading level
    type: choice
    choices: [Grade 6, Grade 8, Grade 10, No target]
    default: Grade 8
---

# Step 1: Analyse accessibility issues

Review the following text for plain-language accessibility issues. List the
problems as a numbered list. Focus on: sentence length (over 25 words), passive
voice, unexplained jargon or acronyms, abstract nouns where concrete ones would
serve better, and complex nested clauses. Be concise — one clear problem per
line. If the text has no issues, say "No issues found."

```input
{selection}

Step 2: Rewrite for accessibility

Rewrite the text below to fix the issues identified in Step 1. Requirements:

  • Target reading level: {parameters.reading_level}
  • Preserve all factual content
  • Do not add new information

Original text: {selection}

Issues to fix: {step1.output}

format: text
label: Rewritten text
accept_into: selection

Step 1 reads the text and makes a numbered list of problems. Step 2 gets that
list through `{step1.output}`, along with the original text, so the model knows
exactly what to fix. When the user presses Accept, the rewrite replaces the
selection.

### Checking your skill

Always run the validator before you share a skill:

```powershell
python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator my-skill.sqp

For a stricter check:

python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator my-skill.sqp --strict

With --strict, it also warns you if description or author is missing.

These are the errors people meet most, and how to fix them:

Error Cause Fix
schema must be 'quill.skill/1' Missing or wrong schema Add schema: quill.skill/1 to front matter
front matter must include 'name' No name: field Add name: My Skill
must have at least one step No # Heading lines Add at least one # Step N: heading
{step3.output} references a step that hasn't run yet Forward reference Steps can only reference outputs from earlier steps
unknown parameter 'tone' Used {parameters.tone} but didn’t declare it Add tone to the parameters list in front matter
output format 'xml' is invalid Bad format: value Use text, list, or json

Sharing skills

A .sqp file is plain text, so you can share it the same way you share any document. There are three ways it reaches other people:

  • Through the Skill Library. Whoever receives your .sqp file imports it with AI > Skill Library > Import .sqp.
  • Through a Quillin. If you look after a Quillin, put your .sqp files in the Quillin’s folder. QUILL finds them on its own when the Skill Library loads.
  • As a file on its own. A .sqp file holds everything it needs. Anyone can also open it in QUILL’s editor to read it, understand it and change any step.

Tips for writing good skills

  • Be specific in each step. “List the five most important claims” works better than “What are the claims?” The model follows precise wording.
  • Say exactly what you want back. Instead of “Summarise the following”, write “Write a one-sentence summary of the following text. Return only the summary sentence, no preamble.” Then {step1.output} holds just what you expect.
  • Try it on short text first. Type two or three sentences into the editor, select them, and run the skill. Short text runs faster, and mistakes are easier to track down.
  • Put long data in an input block. If the selection might be a whole document, put {document} in an input block instead of in the middle of the prompt. The step reads more cleanly.
  • Give a branch its own detection step. If you are branching on whether the text is a question, a statement, a list or something else, let step 1 do only that sorting, and ask for a one-word answer. The tighter the answer, the more reliably the condition works.
  • Choose accept_into on purpose. If the skill rewrites the selection, use accept_into: selection. If it makes something extra (a meeting summary, an outline), use accept_into: clipboard, so the user can paste it where they like. Use none for skills that only inform you (a grammar analysis, a readability score), where you read the result but do not insert it.

Reference card

Front matter fields

Field Required Default
schema: quill.skill/1 yes none
name: ... yes none
description: ... recommended ""
author: ... recommended ""
version: ... no 1.0.0
parameters: [...] no []

Variables

Variable Value
{selection} Selected editor text (full document if nothing selected)
{document} Full document text
{title} Document title
{clipboard} Clipboard text at skill-start time
{stepN.output} Output from step N (must be a lower-numbered step)
{parameters.name} Value of a declared parameter

Fenced block types

Block Where Purpose
`input` Any step Appends data to the prompt
`condition` Any step Branch to then/else step after this step runs
`output` Last step Controls format, label, accept_into
`use-prompt` Any step Delegates to a named Prompt Library prompt

Values at a glance

  • Condition operators: contains, equals, starts_with, ends_with, length_gt, length_lt, is_empty.
  • Output formats: text, list, json.
  • Output accept_into values: selection, clipboard, none.

Where to go next

Open the Skill Library from the AI menu and run one of the skills that come with QUILL, then open its .sqp file and see how it was put together. Chapter 10, AI, when you want it, covers the rest of the assistant.
